docs.title: UniEnv
docs.text:
UniEnv is a robotics-oriented interface layer for environments, worlds, data pipelines, and backend-aware transformations.

It is built to let the same codebase span:

  • simulation environments and real-world control loops
  • stateful and functional environment styles
  • structured observations and flattened tensor views
  • online interaction and offline dataset workflows
  • multiple array backends through a shared compute abstraction

docs.title: Why UniEnv
docs.text:
UniEnv gives you one vocabulary for the parts that tend to fragment robotics codebases:

  • Environment APIs for reset, step, render, and typed spaces
  • World composition for building environments from reusable nodes
  • Policy APIs (Policy, FuncPolicy) that act against the same spaces as the environment
  • Wrappers and transformations for action scaling, flattening, frame stacking, backend conversion, and recording
  • Data interfaces for replay buffers, storage backends, and dataset adapters

The result is a package that can sit between your simulator, robot stack, dataset format, and learning code without forcing each layer to invent its own data model.

docs.title: Reading Order
docs.text:
If you are new to the project, a good path is:

  1. Read Getting Started.
  2. Read Environments and Spaces and Backends.
  3. Read World Composition if you are composing complex simulators or robot systems.
  4. Read Wrappers and Transformations and Replay Buffers and Storage for day-to-day usage.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page is the fastest way to orient yourself in the UniEnvPy package.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install the base package:

pip install unienv

Install optional extras when you need them:

pip install "unienv[gymnasium,video]"

The project also exposes optional integrations and storage backends that depend on external packages such as torch, jax, pyarrow, h5py, datasets, or huggingface_hub. Install those separately when you use the matching modules.

docs.title: The Two Main Namespaces
docs.text:
• unienv_interface: online interaction APIs such as spaces, environments, worlds, wrappers, and transformations
  • unienv_data: offline data APIs such as batches, replay buffers, storage backends, samplers, and dataset adapters
  • unienv_policy: policy interfaces (stateful Policy, functional FuncPolicy) and their wrappers

If you are only building environments, most of your work will start in unienv_interface.

If you are only building dataset or replay-buffer tooling, most of your work will start in unienv_data.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
UniEnv is easiest to understand as four layers:

  1. Spaces describe what valid data looks like.
  2. Environments and worlds produce or consume that data over time.
  3. Wrappers and transformations reshape the interface without changing your core implementation.
  4. Replay buffers and dataset adapters store, sample, and serve the resulting trajectories or transitions.

docs.title: Smallest Useful Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from unienv_interface.backends.numpy import NumpyComputeBackend
from unienv_interface.space.spaces import BoxSpace, DictSpace
from unienv_data.replay_buffer import ReplayBuffer
from unienv_data.storages.parquet import ParquetStorage

backend = NumpyComputeBackend

transition_space = DictSpace(
    backend,
    {
        "obs": BoxSpace(backend, 0.0, 1.0, np.float32, shape=(4,)),
        "action": BoxSpace(backend, -1.0, 1.0, np.float32, shape=(2,)),
    },
)

buffer = ReplayBuffer.create(
    ParquetStorage,
    transition_space,
    cache_path="cache/demo_buffer",
    capacity=1_000,
)

print(buffer.single_space)

If you are logging online, use append() for each step and mark_segment_end() when the segment closes. Segment-aware storages can then report logical ranges through get_segments().

This already shows the basic pattern:

  • define the structure of one sample with a Space
  • build storage around that space
  • keep higher-level code generic over the exact backend or storage implementation

docs.text:

  • Read Spaces and Backends if you need structured data validation or cross-backend movement.
  • Read Replay Buffers and Storage if your next step is logging or offline learning.

docs.title: SpaceStorage
docs.text:
SpaceStorage(single_instance_space: Space[BatchT, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType])

Bases: ABC, Generic[BatchT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

SpaceStorage is an abstract base class for storages that hold instances of a specific space. It provides a common interface for creating, loading, and managing the storage of instances of a given space. Note that if you want your space storage to support multiprocessing, you need to check / implement __getstate__ and __setstate__ methods to ensure that the storage can be pickled and unpickled correctly.

Bind the storage to the space of one stored element.

docs.title: SegmentWriter
docs.text:
SegmentWriter(storage: SpaceStorage)

Bases: ABC

Builds one contiguous segment of a storage off to the side. Values appended to a writer land at an index range that is only chosen when the writer is committed, so several writers of one storage can be filled at the same time (e.g. one per environment of a batched rollout) and committed in any order. Obtain one with SpaceStorage.open_segment_writer().

docs.text:
fill_data_with_stack_mask(
    space: Optional[Space[Any, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]],
    data: Union[BArrayType, BatchT, Any],
    valid_mask: BArrayType,
) -> Union[BArrayType, BatchT, Any]

Fill the data with the mask as if the frames were frame-stacked.

data is updated in place where the backend allows it (backend.at(...).set; JAX and read-only arrays are copied). This is safe because data is the result of fetching an index array from the wrapped batch, a fresh gather: batches wrapped by a SliceStackedBatch must not return arrays aliasing their storage from get_at* / get_flattened_at* with index arrays. Args: space (Optional[Space]): The space to fill the data with. If None, the data is assumed to be a backend array. data (Union[BArrayType, BatchT, Any]): The data to fill sized (B, T, *D) valid_mask (BArrayType): The mask to fill the data with, sized (B, T) Returns: Union[BArrayType, BatchT, Any]: The filled data, sized (B, T, *D)

docs.text:
get_column(nested_keys: Sequence[Any]) -> BatchBase

Lazy view over one field of the stacked samples.

Stacks self.batch.get_column(nested_keys) instead of stacking whole samples and dropping the other fields afterwards, so only that column (plus the episode column the built-in valid-mask helpers read) is gathered. Values, spaces, metadata and the flattened layout are those of SubItemBatch(self, nested_keys), which is returned when that is not possible (a custom valid mask function, which may read any field, a mask read from metadata, or a column view with different metadata).

Samples mini-batches of individual steps (uniformly, with replacement) from data.

Performance notes:

  • For data held in RAM (e.g. an in-memory ReplayBuffer and views over it), sampling in-process is usually faster than MultiprocessingSampler: worker processes only pay off when producing a batch is expensive (decoding, transformations, storage reads), since every batch is copied to the main process.

  • Read single fields through data.get_column(keys) rather than sampling whole samples.

docs.text:
MultiprocessingSampler(
    sampler: BatchSampler[
        SamplerBatchT,
        SamplerArrayType,
        SamplerDeviceType,
        SamplerDtypeType,
        SamplerRNGType,
        BatchT,
        BArrayType,
        BDeviceType,
        BDtypeType,
        BRNGType,
    ],
    n_workers: int = 4,
    n_buffers: int = 8,
    ctx: Optional[BaseContext] = None,
    doze_time: float = 0.005,
    daemon: Optional[bool] = None,
    shared_memory: bool = False,
)

Bases: BatchSampler[SamplerBatchT, SamplerArrayType, SamplerDeviceType, SamplerDtypeType, SamplerRNGType, BatchT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Run sampler's sample* functions (and epoch iteration over its get*_at functions) in n_workers background processes, keeping n_buffers batches queued.

Workers pay off when producing a batch is expensive (decoding, transformations, storage reads). For data already in RAM (e.g. an in-memory ReplayBuffer), sampling in-process is usually faster (e.g. 0.7 ms vs 3 ms for 256 samples of 48 KiB with 4 workers): every batch is otherwise copied to the parent through shared memory. Workers run their torch ops single-threaded (see _limit_worker_intraop_threads).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default shared_memory bool

For sample() / sample_with_metadata() of samplers producing torch CPU tensors, workers copy each batch into one of n_buffers + 1 pre-allocated shared-memory slots and the parent copies it out, instead of sending every tensor through the result queue (a new shared-memory file and file descriptor per tensor and batch). This pays off when batches arrive at a high rate (e.g. ~2x for 64 samples of 48 KiB); for large batches the copy out of the slot in this process can cost more than it saves, so it is off by default.

False

    storage: SpaceStorage[BatchT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType],
    storage_path_relative: str,
    count: int = 0,
    offset: int = 0,
    cache_path: Optional[Union[str, PathLike]] = None,

Bases: BatchBase[BatchT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Ring-buffer style batch storage built on top of a SpaceStorage.

The buffer exposes the standard BatchBase interface while handling round-robin overwrite semantics, persistence metadata, and optional multiprocessing-safe counters.

With multiprocessing=True writers serialize on a shared lock and publish count and offset together; readers in other processes take no lock and always map indices with a consistent pair. A read that races with a write can still return rows that the write is overwriting (the oldest samples of a full buffer), as with any lock-free ring buffer.

Wrap a storage object with replay-buffer indexing semantics.

open_segment_writer() -> SegmentWriter

A writer that builds one segment off to the side; commit_segment() then appends it at the tail. Unlike append() / mark_segment_end(), any number of writers can be open at a time (e.g. one per environment of a batched rollout), and they can be committed in any order. Storages that support it (e.g. VideoStorage) encode the samples as they are appended.

env : Env The environment to wrap. replay_buffers : ReplayBuffer | Sequence[ReplayBuffer] One replay buffer (shared mode) or one per environment slot (per‑env mode). replay_mode : "auto", "shared" or "per_env" * "shared" - a single flat replay buffer. * "per_env" - one buffer per batched slot, with episode segments. * "auto" - resolve based on batch_size and buffer count. transition_builder : callable or DataTransformation, optional Either a callable (cached_obs, cached_context, action, next_obs, reward, terminated, truncated, env_index, rb_single_space) -> transition, or a DataTransformation that maps a canonical raw transition dict to the replay buffer's format. Requires dump_path to be set. dump_on_reset_boundary : bool When True, automatically call dumps(path) on reset boundaries (full reset or masked reset). Requires dump_path to be set. dump_path : str | os.PathLike | None Filesystem path where the replay buffer(s) should be dumped when auto-dump is triggered. May be reassigned after construction to redirect subsequent dumps. Required if dump_on_episode_end or dump_on_reset_boundary is True. Repeated dumps overwrite the same path.

docs.title: SegmentWriter
docs.text:
SegmentWriter(storage: SpaceStorage)

Bases: ABC

Builds one contiguous segment of a storage off to the side. Values appended to a writer land at an index range that is only chosen when the writer is committed, so several writers of one storage can be filled at the same time (e.g. one per environment of a batched rollout) and committed in any order. Obtain one with SpaceStorage.open_segment_writer().

Bases: ABC, Generic[BatchT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

SpaceStorage is an abstract base class for storages that hold instances of a specific space. It provides a common interface for creating, loading, and managing the storage of instances of a given space. Note that if you want your space storage to support multiprocessing, you need to check / implement __getstate__ and __setstate__ methods to ensure that the storage can be pickled and unpickled correctly.

This batch allows for prefetching and postfetching of frames, which can be useful for training models that require temporal context (e.g. Diffusion Policy, ACT, etc.) This is a read-only batch, since it is a view of the original batch. If you want to change the data, you should mutate the containing batch instead.

get_column(nested_keys: Sequence[Any]) -> BatchBase

Lazy view over one field of the stacked samples.

Stacks self.batch.get_column(nested_keys) instead of stacking whole samples and dropping the other fields afterwards, so only that column (plus the episode column the built-in valid-mask helpers read) is gathered. Values, spaces, metadata and the flattened layout are those of SubItemBatch(self, nested_keys), which is returned when that is not possible (a custom valid mask function, which may read any field, a mask read from metadata, or a column view with different metadata).

docs.title: fill_data_with_stack_mask
docs.text:
fill_data_with_stack_mask(
    space: Optional[Space[Any, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]],
    data: Union[BArrayType, BatchT, Any],
    valid_mask: BArrayType,
) -> Union[BArrayType, BatchT, Any]

Fill the data with the mask as if the frames were frame-stacked.

data is updated in place where the backend allows it (backend.at(...).set; JAX and read-only arrays are copied). This is safe because data is the result of fetching an index array from the wrapped batch, a fresh gather: batches wrapped by a SliceStackedBatch must not return arrays aliasing their storage from get_at* / get_flattened_at* with index arrays. Args: space (Optional[Space]): The space to fill the data with. If None, the data is assumed to be a backend array. data (Union[BArrayType, BatchT, Any]): The data to fill sized (B, T, *D) valid_mask (BArrayType): The mask to fill the data with, sized (B, T) Returns: Union[BArrayType, BatchT, Any]: The filled data, sized (B, T, *D)

Bases: Dataset

A PyTorch Dataset wrapper for UniEnvPy batches. __getitems__ fetches a whole mini-batch with a single (already collated) batch access, so PyTorch's default collation must be bypassed: pass collate_fn=UniEnvAsPyTorchDataset.collate_fn (the identity) to the DataLoader. Note that collate_fn=None selects PyTorch's default_collate, which cannot handle a pre-collated batch.

Example::

loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True, collate_fn=dataset.collate_fn)

docs.title: unienv_data.replay_buffer.collection_wrapper
docs.text:
ReplayBufferCollectionWrapper – transparently records transitions into replay buffers.

This wrapper sits around any Env and writes every step transition into one or more ReplayBuffer instances according to the chosen replay_mode.

docs.title: Environment-space invariant
docs.text:
This wrapper relies on the :class:~unienv_interface.env_base.env.Env contract that when an env is batched, its observation_space, action_space, and context_space already include the leading batch dimension. The internal source/target space builders (_build_canonical_source_space and the default DictSpace builder) therefore use the env-side spaces as-is and never wrap them in an additional batch_space call. Re-batching those spaces would double-batch and produce incorrect shapes – this was the root cause of a previous bug in this module.

Name Description ReplayBufferCollectionWrapper

Automatically record every transition into one or more replay buffers.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
env : Env The environment to wrap. replay_buffers : ReplayBuffer | Sequence[ReplayBuffer] One replay buffer (shared mode) or one per environment slot (per‑env mode). replay_mode : "auto", "shared" or "per_env" * "shared" - a single flat replay buffer. * "per_env" - one buffer per batched slot, with episode segments. * "auto" - resolve based on batch_size and buffer count. transition_builder : callable or DataTransformation, optional Either a callable (cached_obs, cached_context, action, next_obs, reward, terminated, truncated, env_index, rb_single_space) -> transition, or a DataTransformation that maps a canonical raw transition dict to the replay buffer's format. When None the default DictSpace‑based builder is used. validate_transition : bool When True every built transition is validated against the target replay buffer's space (single‑instance for append / batched for shared extend). Off by default for speed. dump_on_episode_end : bool When True, automatically call dumps(path) on the replay buffer(s) after an episode ends (i.e., when terminated or truncated is true). Requires dump_path to be set. dump_on_reset_boundary : bool When True, automatically call dumps(path) on reset boundaries (full reset or masked reset). Requires dump_path to be set. dump_path : str | os.PathLike | None Filesystem path where the replay buffer(s) should be dumped when auto-dump is triggered. May be reassigned after construction to redirect subsequent dumps. Required if dump_on_episode_end or dump_on_reset_boundary is True. Repeated dumps overwrite the same path.

Bases: BatchBase[BatchT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Ring-buffer style batch storage built on top of a SpaceStorage.

The buffer exposes the standard BatchBase interface while handling round-robin overwrite semantics, persistence metadata, and optional multiprocessing-safe counters.

With multiprocessing=True writers serialize on a shared lock and publish count and offset together; readers in other processes take no lock and always map indices with a consistent pair. A read that races with a write can still return rows that the write is overwriting (the oldest samples of a full buffer), as with any lock-free ring buffer.

Wrap a storage object with replay-buffer indexing semantics.

Bases: BatchSampler[SamplerBatchT, SamplerArrayType, SamplerDeviceType, SamplerDtypeType, SamplerRNGType, BatchT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Run sampler's sample* functions (and epoch iteration over its get*_at functions) in n_workers background processes, keeping n_buffers batches queued.

Workers pay off when producing a batch is expensive (decoding, transformations, storage reads). For data already in RAM (e.g. an in-memory ReplayBuffer), sampling in-process is usually faster (e.g. 0.7 ms vs 3 ms for 256 samples of 48 KiB with 4 workers): every batch is otherwise copied to the parent through shared memory. Workers run their torch ops single-threaded (see _limit_worker_intraop_threads).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default shared_memory bool

For sample() / sample_with_metadata() of samplers producing torch CPU tensors, workers copy each batch into one of n_buffers + 1 pre-allocated shared-memory slots and the parent copies it out, instead of sending every tensor through the result queue (a new shared-memory file and file descriptor per tensor and batch). This pays off when batches arrive at a high rate (e.g. ~2x for 64 samples of 48 KiB); for large batches the copy out of the slot in this process can cost more than it saves, so it is off by default.

False

Samples mini-batches of individual steps (uniformly, with replacement) from data.

Performance notes:

  • For data held in RAM (e.g. an in-memory ReplayBuffer and views over it), sampling in-process is usually faster than MultiprocessingSampler: worker processes only pay off when producing a batch is expensive (decoding, transformations, storage reads), since every batch is copied to the main process.
  • sample_flat() / get_flattened_at() flatten a sample into one array of a common dtype, so uint8 images next to float32 fields are cast to float32 (4x the bytes and a conversion per batch). Prefer sample() for image data.
  • Read single fields through data.get_column(keys) rather than sampling whole samples.

Bases: SpaceStorage[BatchT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Stores every sample flattened into one 1D BoxSpace row of an inner storage (e.g. PytorchTensorStorage), so a read or write is one row operation on a single array.

The flat row has one common dtype, promoted from all leaves: mixing uint8 camera images with float32 keys stores the images as float32 (4x the memory / disk of uint8, e.g. 1.97 GB instead of 0.49 GB for 10k 128x128x3 frames) and converts every image on every read and write. Keep images in their own storage instead, e.g. a DictStorage with a PytorchTensorStorage (or VideoStorage) per image key, and flatten only the low-dimensional keys.

Bases: SpaceStorage[HDF5BatchType, NumpyArrayType, NumpyDeviceType, NumpyDtypeType, NumpyRNGType]

Stores samples of a (nested) DictSpace / BoxSpace / BinarySpace / TextSpace in one HDF5 file, one dataset per leaf, numpy backend only.

Dataset layout, chosen by create() from chunks / compression (a mapping sets them per key, "*" for the remaining keys):

  • Fixed capacity, no compression, chunks=None (the default): contiguous datasets, the fastest layout for per-step appends and random reads.
  • chunks=None or chunks=True with compression, or an unbounded storage: chunks of whole rows of about CHUNK_TARGET_BYTES (64 KiB), e.g. one 128x128x3 uint8 image or ~2300 7-float rows per chunk, so a row access touches (and decompresses) a single chunk. Compressed files come out somewhat larger than with h5py's sub-row chunk guess, which made every image read decompress dozens of chunks.
  • An explicit tuple is used as given, padded with the row shape: chunks=(1,) stores every step in its own chunk (the per-step layout: cheapest single-row writes and reads with compression, worst ratio).

Compression ("gzip", "lzf") trades write and random-read speed for size. For camera images prefer VideoStorage (or ImageStorage with JPEG / PNG) over gzip-compressed HDF5; keep low-dim keys uncompressed.

docs.title: unienv_data.storages.metadata_routing
docs.text:
Build a DictStorage layout from the Space.metadata of a DictSpace.

Camera images are best stored by an image / video storage, everything else by a tensor storage. Instead of listing the keys by hand::

from unienv_data.replay_buffer import ReplayBuffer
from unienv_data.storages import DictStorage, dict_storage_kwargs_from_space

rb = ReplayBuffer.create(
    DictStorage, obs_space,
    cache_path="cache/rb", capacity=None,
    **dict_storage_kwargs_from_space(obs_space),
)

routes every kind == "image" uint8 leaf of obs_space to an ImageStorage and the remaining leaves to one HDF5Storage.

Functions:

Name Description dict_storage_kwargs_from_space

DictStorage.create keyword arguments that route each leaf of space by its metadata.

docs.title: dict_storage_kwargs_from_space
docs.text:
dict_storage_kwargs_from_space(
    space: DictSpace,
    *,
    kind_storage_cls: Optional[Mapping[str, Optional[Type[SpaceStorage]]]] = None,
    key_storage_cls: Optional[Mapping[str, Optional[Type[SpaceStorage]]]] = None,
    default_storage_cls: Optional[Type[SpaceStorage]] = None,
    kind_kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]]] = None,
    key_kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]]] = None,
    default_kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None,
    nested_separator: str = "/",
) -> Dict[str, Any]

DictStorage.create keyword arguments that route each leaf of space by its metadata.

Every leaf of the (nested) DictSpace is assigned, in order of precedence:

  1. key_storage_cls[key] if its key (nested keys joined by nested_separator) is listed (None sends it to the default storage);
  2. kind_storage_cls[leaf.metadata["kind"]] if its kind is listed and the storage can take it. The default is {"image": ImageStorage}, i.e. JPEG files (ImageStorage's defaults; use kind_kwargs={"image": {"format": "PNG"}} for lossless files or map "image" to VideoStorage). Image leaves must be (H, W, 3) uint8 with an "HWC" (or undeclared) layout, others (e.g. CHW or float images) go to the default storage;
  3. otherwise the default storage, default_storage_cls (HDF5Storage if not given, which needs h5py and a NumPy-backend space), which receives all remaining leaves as one DictSpace (key "*").

Keyword arguments for the sub-storages are merged from kind_kwargs[kind] and key_kwargs[key] (default_kwargs / key_kwargs["*"] for the default storage). A VideoStorage leaf whose metadata declares fps gets it as the fps argument unless one is given.

Returns {"storage_cls_map", "key_kwargs", "nested_separator"}, to be passed as ReplayBuffer.create(DictStorage, space, **kwargs) or DictStorage.create(space, **kwargs). Image and video storages write files, so a cache_path is required when any leaf is routed to one.

Bases: SpaceStorage[ParquetBatchType, NumpyArrayType, NumpyDeviceType, NumpyDtypeType, NumpyRNGType]

Stores samples of a flat DictSpace (or a single BoxSpace / BinarySpace / TextSpace) as a directory of Parquet files ("pieces") of piece_size rows each, plus _metadata.json. Numpy backend only.

A mutable storage keeps the pieces it touches in memory and rewrites a whole piece when it flushes it: on dumps() / close() / pickling, and, while an unbounded storage grows, every piece as soon as it is complete. The last, partial piece of a growing storage is only written by dumps() / close(); until then the directory holds a loadable prefix of the data (complete pieces, or what the last dumps() wrote).

Parquet suits low-dimensional, columnar data that other tools read too. It is a poor fit for images: every flush re-encodes whole pieces of pixels, and reads decode whole columns of a piece. Store camera frames in VideoStorage / ImageStorage (e.g. through a DictStorage) and keep the low-dim keys here.

Create a storage directory at cache_path.

array_encoding sets how columns holding an array per row are stored, for all of them or per column (a mapping from column names to encodings, "*" for the rest):

  • "list" (default): a fixed-size list of numbers, which pandas, Hugging Face datasets, DuckDB and other Parquet readers load as arrays.
  • "binary": one fixed-size binary value per row holding the array's little-endian bytes. Writing and reading are ~8-10x faster for large arrays such as images (the list encoding pays per element), at the same file size, but other tools see opaque bytes, and UniEnv versions before this option cannot read the files.

The encodings are recorded in _metadata.json; load_from reads both.

Bases: EpisodeStorageBase[BArrayType, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

A storage for RGB or depth video data using video files If encoding RGB video - Set buffer_pixel_format to rgb24 - Set file_pixel_format to None (especially when running with nvenc codec) - Set file_ext to anything you like (e.g., "mp4", "avi", "mkv", etc.) If encoding depth video - Set buffer_pixel_format to gray16le (You can use rescale transform inside a TransformedStorage to convert depth values to this format, where dtype should be np.uint16) - if in meters, set min to 0 and max to 65.535 as the multiplication factor is 1000 (i.e., depth in mm) - Set file_pixel_format to gray16le - Set codec to a lossless codec that supports gray16le, e.g., ffv1 - Set file_ext to mkv encoder_options are passed to the encoder (e.g. {"crf": "28", "g": "15"}) and persisted in the metadata, so a loaded storage keeps encoding new segments the same way.

Random access: reading frame i decodes from the keyframe at or before i, so the cost of a random read grows with the GOP size (keyframe interval). Encoders default to long GOPs (libx264: 250 frames, i.e. one keyframe per episode); for buffers sampled at random positions set a short one, e.g. encoder_options={"g": "15"} (larger files, much cheaper random reads). Sequential and dense reads are not affected, and sparse reads within one file decode forward instead of seeking when no keyframe lies between two requested frames (the PyAV reader indexes each file's keyframes once).

docs.title: Env
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[BArrayType, ContextType, ObsType, ActType, RenderFrame, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Stateful environment interface used throughout UniEnv.

An Env exposes typed action, observation, and optional context spaces plus the standard reset/step/render lifecycle. Concrete implementations may be single-instance or batched depending on batch_size.

docs.title: Batched-environment space invariant
docs.text:
The observation_space, action_space, and context_space (when present) always describe the data that the environment actually returns and accepts – including any batch dimension.

  • batch_size is None → the environment is unbatched. The spaces describe single-instance values (no leading batch axis).
  • batch_size == N (including N == 1) → the environment is batched with a leading batch dimension of size N. The spaces already include that leading batch dimension. Callers, wrappers, and downstream code must not apply an additional batch_space (or equivalent) on top of these spaces – doing so would double-batch and produce incorrect shapes.

This invariant matters whenever code builds source/target spaces from the env (e.g. replay-buffer builders, data transformations, or wrappers that unbatch per-slot data): always use the env-side spaces as-is and only unbatch/slice the data, never re-batch the space.

docs.text:
AsyncVecEnv(
    env_fn: Iterable[
        Callable[
            [],
            Env[
                BArrayType,
                ContextType,
                ObsType,
                ActType,
                RenderFrame,
                BDeviceType,
                BDtypeType,
                BRNGType,
            ],
        ]
    ],
    seed: Optional[int] = None,
    ctx: Optional[BaseContext] = None,
    daemon: bool = True,
    shared_memory: bool = True,
    copy: bool = True,
)

Bases: Env[BArrayType, ContextType, ObsType, ActType, RenderFrame, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Run multiple non-batched environments in separate worker processes.

Seeding follows :class:SyncVecEnv: reset(seed=s) resets worker i with seed s + i. If a worker raises, the exception is re-raised in the parent as a RuntimeError (chained to the worker's exception) and that worker process exits.

No environment is built in the parent process: the spaces, backend, device, metadata and render settings are reported by the workers (spaces travel as :func:space_to_json payloads, so this works with every start method), and the constructor raises if a worker fails to build its environment or if the workers disagree on backend or device. Differing sub-environment spaces are batched like in :class:SyncVecEnv.

Shared memory (shared_memory=True, the default): the parent allocates one buffer of shape (num_envs, *leaf_shape) per leaf of the single-env observation, context and action spaces. Worker i writes its observation / context into row i and reads its action from row i (step writes the whole action batch once and sends a payload-free command), so only reward, termination flags and info travel through the pipe and nothing is pickled or concatenated. Each group (observation, context, action) that cannot be shared falls back to the pipe on its own, with one INFO message on the unienv_interface.env_base.vec_env logger; :attr:shared_groups lists the groups that are shared. shared_memory=False sends everything through the pipe. Where the buffers live follows the worker env:

================ =============================== ================================= worker env buffer parent read ================ =============================== ================================= numpy host shared memory zero-copy numpy view torch CPU host shared memory zero-copy torch view torch CUDA CUDA buffer owned by the zero-copy on the GPU parent, shared via CUDA IPC jax CPU host shared memory copy=True: one copy into a fresh jax array; copy=False: zero-copy via DLPack (falls back to a copy if XLA refuses) jax GPU the same CUDA IPC buffer, with zero-copy via DLPack torch as carrier (DLPack in/out) jax TPU / other host shared memory (the worker one host-to-device transfer per devices copies device -> host) read ================ =============================== =================================

Actions use the same buffers in the other direction; every worker hands its env a private copy of its row.

Details of shared mode:

  • Only fixed-size spaces can be shared: BoxSpace / BinarySpace leaves nested in DictSpace / TupleSpace (other groups use the pipe). Observations and contexts must match their declared space exactly (shape and dtype per leaf); a mismatch raises in the worker and surfaces as the usual chained RuntimeError naming the leaf, nothing is cast silently (fix the env or pass shared_memory=False). Actions must have shape (num_envs, *action_leaf_shape); their dtype is cast with same-kind rules (e.g. float64 policy outputs into a float32 space). info always travels through the pipe.
  • copy=True (default) returns data that never changes afterwards. copy=False returns the shared buffers themselves (or zero-copy views of them): they are only valid until the next step / reset (which overwrite them in place) and must not be written to; copy anything you want to keep, and make sure asynchronous consumers (e.g. JAX computations) have finished before the next call. CUDA buffers are synchronised by the parent before every step / reset. Masked resets always return freshly gathered rows.
  • Every start method works. With fork (the Linux default) CUDA IPC works as long as the parent had not initialised CUDA before the workers were forked (no env is built in the parent, so that is the usual case); otherwise the workers cannot use CUDA at all, which torch reports when they build their env - use spawn / forkserver then. CUDA IPC is Linux-only; elsewhere CUDA buffers are staged through host shared memory (with a warning). JAX GPU envs need PyTorch as the IPC carrier and a CUDA-enabled jaxlib in the parent (otherwise they use the pipe). A TPU belongs to a single process, so TPU envs cannot be shared: run the workers on the host (or let them copy to the host) and the parent performs one host-to-TPU transfer per read.
  • Workers set XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false unless the variable is already set, so that N JAX workers do not each reserve 75% of the GPU.
  • The parent owns the buffers until :meth:close, which first shuts the workers down; host shared memory is unlinked on close (also after a worker crash) and when the env is garbage collected, and shared-memory envs that are still open at interpreter exit are closed then. Views returned with copy=False stay readable after close (the mapping is released with the last view). A worker that is killed hard (e.g. SIGKILL) cannot release its CUDA IPC references, in which case torch may warn about it when the parent exits.

Spawn worker processes and batch the spaces they report.

Base class for stateful environment wrappers.

The wrapper forwards all operations to env by default while allowing subclasses to override spaces, RNG handling, and selected lifecycle methods.

docs.title: Space-forwarding invariant
docs.text:
By default the wrapper exposes the wrapped env's action_space, observation_space, and context_space unchanged. Because the :class:Env contract guarantees that these spaces already include the batch dimension when the env is batched, subclasses that do override a space must ensure the replacement still matches the batching status of the underlying env. Never wrap an already-batched env space in an additional batch_space call.

Wrap env and optionally override spaces or metadata later.

Functional environment interface with explicit immutable state passing.

Unlike :class:Env, a FuncEnv never stores simulation state on the instance. Instead, every lifecycle method takes a state object and returns the updated state explicitly, which makes the interface easier to compose with JAX-style functional code.

docs.title: Space-forwarding invariant
docs.text:
By default the wrapper forwards the wrapped FuncEnv's action_space, observation_space, and context_space unchanged. Because the :class:FuncEnv contract guarantees that these spaces already include the batch dimension when the env is batched, subclasses that override a space must ensure the replacement still matches the batching status of the underlying env. docs.text:
reload(
    *, seed: Optional[int] = None, mask: Optional[BArrayType] = None, **kwargs

Prepare the world for reloading. This is called BEFORE nodes add entities.

Use this hook to: - Clear old scene data - Load asset definitions - Prepare for entities to be added by nodes

DO NOT compile the scene here. Compilation happens in after_reload() after all nodes have had a chance to add their entities.

By default, this just calls reset with the same parameters. Simulation environments should override this to prepare for entity addition.

The reload flow is
  1. world.reload() # World prepares (clear, load assets)
  2. node.reload() # Nodes add entities to scene
  3. world.after_reload() # World compiles scene with all entities
  4. node.after_reload() # Nodes cache references

docs.title: WorldNode
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[ContextType, ObsType, ActType, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

A stateful node that manages one aspect of a world (e.g. a sensor, a robot, a reward function).

The environment is initialized during the first call to reset or reload.

Lifecycle — reset flow::

World.reset()
  -> WorldNode.reset(priority=...)
  -> WorldNode.after_reset(priority=...)
  -> WorldNode.get_context() / get_observation() / get_info() / render()

Lifecycle — reload flow::

World.reload()
  -> WorldNode.reload(priority=...)
  -> WorldNode.after_reset(priority=...)
  -> WorldNode.get_context() / get_observation() / get_info() / render()

reload re-generates the simulation environment (e.g. re-reading assets, rebuilding the scene). This is typically much more expensive than reset and should only be called when the environment configuration has changed. By default reload delegates to reset.

Lifecycle — step flow::

WorldNode.set_next_action(action)
  -> WorldNode.pre_environment_step(dt, priority=...)
  -> World.step()
  -> WorldNode.post_environment_step(dt, priority=...)
  -> WorldNode.get_observation()
  -> WorldNode.get_reward() / get_termination() / get_truncation() / get_info() / render()

docs.title: Implementing a node
docs.text:
Subclasses should:

  1. Set name, world, and any relevant spaces / signal flags / render attributes (render_mode, supported_render_modes) in __init__.
  2. Override the lifecycle methods they need (reset, pre_environment_step, etc.).
  3. Populate the corresponding priority sets for every lifecycle method they override. Callers check these sets before dispatching a method call — a node will only have a given method called for priorities present in its corresponding set. A node with an empty priority set for a given method will never have that method called.

Example::

   class MySensor(WorldNode[...]):
       after_reset_priorities = {0}
       post_environment_step_priorities = {0}

       def post_environment_step(self, dt, *, priority=0):
           ...  # read sensor data

Multiple priorities (e.g. {0, 1}) allow the same method to be invoked at different stages; the caller iterates priorities in the desired order.

docs.title: Space lifecycle contract
docs.text:
action_space, observation_space, and context_space follow a two-phase lifecycle:

Phase 1 — construction (__init__): Nodes should expose a preliminary space if the dimensionality is known before the scene is built. For example, an EEF controller always produces a 6-D action regardless of the number of robot DOFs, so the space can be set to a BoxSpace with [-inf, inf] bounds immediately. If the dimensionality is genuinely unknown (e.g. a joint-position controller whose DOF count comes from the compiled scene), the space may be None at this stage.

Phase 2 — post-build (end of after_reload): By the time the lowest-priority after_reload has returned, every node must have set its final, tightly-bounded spaces. CombinedWorldNode calls _refresh_spaces() at this point so that the aggregated spaces seen by the environment composer reflect the true, post-build state.

Priority conventions (in reload / reset / after_reload / after_reset): Higher priority runs first (sorted(..., reverse=True)).

  • [100, 200) -> Floor / surrounding environment setup (e.g. table, ground plane)
  • [50, 100) -> Robot setup (add URDF/MJCF entity, init controller, apply rest pose)
  • [0, 50) -> Object / prop setup; general post-step observation updates
  • (-, 0) -> Sensors / renderers that must run after all entities are settled (e.g. cameras: -50)

docs.title: reload
docs.text:
reload(state: WorldStateT, *, seed: Optional[int] = None, **kwargs) -> WorldStateT

Prepare the world for reloading. This is called BEFORE nodes add entities.

Use this hook to: - Clear old scene data - Load asset definitions - Prepare for entities to be added by nodes

DO NOT compile the scene here. Compilation happens in after_reload() after all nodes have had a chance to add their entities.

By default, this just calls initial with the same parameters. Simulation environments should override this to prepare for entity addition.

The reload flow is
  1. world.reload() # World prepares (clear, load assets)
  2. node.reload() # Nodes add entities to scene
  3. world.after_reload() # World compiles scene with all entities
  4. node.after_reload() # Nodes cache references

docs.title: FuncWorldNode
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[WorldStateT, NodeStateT, ContextType, ObsType, ActType, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

A functional (stateless) node that manages one aspect of a world.

Unlike WorldNode, every method receives and returns explicit state objects (world_state, node_state) instead of mutating internal attributes.

initial creates the node state for the first time (the environment has not been set up yet). reset is called on subsequent episode boundaries when the node state already exists.

Lifecycle — initial flow (environment not yet created)::

FuncWorldNode.initial(world_state, priority=...)
  -> returns (world_state, node_state)

Lifecycle — reset flow::

FuncWorld.reset()
  -> FuncWorldNode.reset(world_state, node_state, priority=...)
  -> FuncWorldNode.after_reset(world_state, node_state, priority=...)
  -> FuncWorldNode.get_context(...) / get_observation(...) / get_info(...) / render(...)

Lifecycle — reload flow::

FuncWorld.reload()          # World prepares (clear, load assets)
  -> FuncWorldNode.reload(world_state, priority=...)     # Nodes add entities
FuncWorld.after_reload()    # World compiles scene
  -> FuncWorldNode.after_reload(world_state, node_state, priority=...)  # Nodes cache refs
  -> FuncWorldNode.get_context(...) / get_observation(...) / get_info(...) / render(...)

reload re-generates the simulation environment (e.g. re-reading assets, rebuilding the scene). This is typically much more expensive than reset and should only be called when the environment configuration has changed. By default reload delegates to initial.

Lifecycle — step flow::

FuncWorldNode.set_next_action(world_state, node_state, action)
  -> FuncWorldNode.pre_environment_step(world_state, node_state, dt, priority=...)
  -> FuncWorld.step()
  -> FuncWorldNode.post_environment_step(world_state, node_state, dt, priority=...)
  -> FuncWorldNode.get_observation(world_state, node_state)
  -> FuncWorldNode.get_reward(...) / get_termination(...) / get_truncation(...) / get_info(...) / render(...)

docs.title: Implementing a node
docs.text:
Subclasses should:

  1. Set name, world, and any relevant spaces / signal flags / render attributes (render_mode, supported_render_modes) in __init__ (or as class-level attributes).
  2. Implement initial and reset (both abstract), plus any other lifecycle methods the node needs (pre_environment_step, post_environment_step, etc.).
  3. Populate the corresponding priority sets for every lifecycle method they implement. Callers check these sets before dispatching a method call — a node will only have a given method called for priorities present in its corresponding set. A node with an empty priority set for a given method will never have that method called.

Example::

   class MySensor(FuncWorldNode[...]):
       initial_priorities = {0}
       reset_priorities = {0}
       after_reset_priorities = {0}
       post_environment_step_priorities = {0}

       def initial(self, world_state, *, priority=0, seed=None, **kwargs):
           ...
       def reset(self, world_state, node_state, *, priority=0, seed=None, mask=None, **kwargs):
           ...

Multiple priorities (e.g. {0, 1}) allow the same method to be invoked at different stages; the caller iterates priorities in the desired order.

docs.title: Space contract
docs.text:
action_space, observation_space, and context_space are static interface metadata. They must be fully declared in __init__ and must not change after construction. CombinedFuncWorldNode reads them once at construction time; there is no refresh mechanism.

Unlike stateful WorldNode subclasses (which may need to build a simulation scene before knowing DOF counts), functional nodes are expected to derive their spaces purely from their configuration parameters.

Bases: WorldNode[ContextType, ObsType, ActType, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Adapt an existing unbatched :class:Env so it can be composed as a WorldNode.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Env.step(action) is atomic: it produces the next observation, reward, termination/truncation signals, and info in a single call. A WorldNode instead splits the step lifecycle into::

set_next_action(action)
  -> pre_environment_step(dt, priority=...)
  -> World.step()
  -> post_environment_step(dt, priority=...)
  -> get_observation() / get_reward() / ... / get_info()

This adapter bridges the mismatch by performing the atomic inner Env.step inside pre_environment_step (using the action cached by the preceding set_next_action call) and caching its five-tuple result for the get_* accessors to expose. reset maps directly to Env.reset, and the base WorldNode.reload default (which delegates to reset) is exactly right for a pre-built environment, hence the non-empty reset_priorities / reload_priorities sets.

The dt argument of pre_environment_step is intentionally ignored: the wrapped environment is self-paced (e.g. real hardware running at its own control rate), while the outer world is expected to be a bookkeeping-only world such as :class:RealWorld. control_timestep / update_timestep can still be set for step-ratio bookkeeping by the composer.

No schema transformation / re-keying is performed: the inner environment's action, observation, and context spaces (and the raw observation / context layouts) pass through unchanged.

Only unbatched environments (batch_size is None) are supported. The optional world is only used for backend/device delegation; when provided its backend type must match the inner environment's backend, since the node serves the inner environment's arrays.

Bases: WorldNode[Optional[CombinedDataT], CombinedDataT, CombinedDataT, BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType], Generic[BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

A WorldNode that combines multiple WorldNodes into one node, using a dictionary to store the data from each node. The observation, reward, termination, truncation, and info are combined from all child nodes. The keys in the dictionary are the names of the child nodes. If there is only one child node that supports value and direct_return is set to True, the value is returned directly instead of a dictionary.

docs.title: Root node
docs.text:
An optional root_node may be passed next to nodes. It is a regular node (sharing the same :class:~unienv_interface.world.world.World) that is NOT part of the public nodes list and whose data merges at the TOP LEVEL of the aggregated dictionaries instead of nesting under its own name. It rides the same machinery as a child node -- priorities, control/update rate ratios, lifecycle dispatch, rewards/signals, info, render and close -- under the reserved internal key :data:ROOT_NODE_KEY (""), which cannot collide with a child node name (child names are validated non-empty).

  • Spaces / data (context, observation, action -- independently). When the root node is the sole contributor of a channel, the existing direct_return rule applies verbatim: direct_return=True passes the root's own space/data through unwrapped (any Space type, e.g. a plain BoxSpace), while direct_return=False wraps it under the reserved key (DictSpace({ROOT_NODE_KEY: space}) / {ROOT_NODE_KEY: data}). When the root and at least one named child contribute, the root MUST expose a DictSpace for that channel and its keys are merged next to the child entries: {child_name: child_space, ..., **root_space.spaces} (resp. {child_name: child_data, ..., **root_data}). A root key equal to a child node name raises ValueError.
  • Actions. For a sole-root action channel the aggregate action space is the root's action space and the whole action value is forwarded to the root at its own control-rate tick. In the mixed case the incoming mapping is routed by key: keys matching action-child names update those children's caches (exactly as before), and every remaining key accumulates into the root's action entry as a dict. Each consumer is dispatched at its own ratio tick with hold-last semantics identical to children.
  • Info / render. These channels nest by node name for children, so the root's entries are keyed by the root's own name (the reserved key is only used for internal state/routing and aggregation).
  • get_node never resolves the reserved key (it is not a user-facing path); get_nodes_by_fn does traverse the root node.

set_next_action(action)

Route combined actions to child nodes (and the optional root node), respecting per-node control rates.

The incoming action is split by :meth:_split_child_actions (children only). When a root_node owns an action space and no single node is the direct-action passthrough provider, the keys that do not belong to any named child are the root's action keys: they accumulate into the root's cache entry under the reserved key as a dict. Every consumer (children and root) is then dispatched at its own ratio tick, and only once it has received at least one action (hold-last semantics, so a child-only step re-delivers the root's previous action at its tick and vice versa).

Bases: CombinedWorldNode[BArrayType, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

A WorldNode that combines multiple WorldNodes and flattens their data.

Unlike CombinedWorldNode which stores data as {node_name: {key: value}}, FlatCombinedWorldNode merges dictionaries directly as {key1: value1, key2: value2}.

This requires: - All nodes with observation/action/context spaces must use DictSpace - Keys across all nodes must be unique (no overlaps)

The node names are only used for identification, not for nesting data.

docs.title: Root node
docs.text:
An optional root_node (passed separately, sharing the same world and not listed in nodes) is handled as one more flat contributor:

  • Its context / observation spaces and data are appended to the flatten list, so its keys appear directly at the top level next to the children's keys (an overlapping key raises ValueError). When the root is the only contributor its space/data is returned unwrapped, mirroring the existing single-child flat behavior.
  • For actions, every key not claimed by any child's action space is routed to the root under the reserved internal key, while claimed keys are sliced to their children exactly as before. Without a root_node such unclaimed keys are rejected with a ValueError.
  • Rewards / signals / info / render and the lifecycle hooks include the root like any other node (info and render use the root's own name).

A functional counterpart to CombinedWorldNode that composes multiple FuncWorldNodes.

It aggregates spaces (context, observation, action) and runtime data (context, observation, info, reward, termination, truncation) across child nodes. If only one child exposes a given interface and direct_return=True, the value is passed through directly.

docs.title: Root node
docs.text:
An optional root_node may be passed next to nodes. It is a regular FuncWorldNode (sharing the same FuncWorld) that is NOT part of the public nodes list and whose data merges at the TOP LEVEL of the aggregated dictionaries instead of nesting under its own name. It rides the same machinery as a child node -- priorities, control/update rate ratios, lifecycle dispatch, rewards/signals, info, render and close -- and its node state is stored in the combined node_state under the reserved key :data:ROOT_NODE_KEY (""), a string key that cannot collide with a child node name (child names are validated non-empty) and therefore keeps persisted CombinedNodeStateT dictionaries loadable without migration.

  • Spaces / data (context, observation, action -- independently). Spaces are aggregated once at construction (functional nodes declare static spaces). When the root node is the sole contributor of a channel, the existing direct_return rule applies verbatim: direct_return=True passes the root's own space/data through unwrapped (any Space type, e.g. a plain BoxSpace), while direct_return=False wraps it under the reserved key (DictSpace({ROOT_NODE_KEY: space}) / {ROOT_NODE_KEY: data}). When the root and at least one named child contribute, the root MUST expose a DictSpace for that channel and its keys are merged next to the child entries: {child_name: child_space, ..., **root_space.spaces} (resp. {child_name: child_data, ..., **root_data}). A root key equal to a child node name raises ValueError.
  • Actions. For a sole-root action channel the aggregate action space is the root's action space and the whole action value is forwarded to the root at its own control-rate tick. In the mixed case the incoming mapping is routed by key: keys matching action-child names update those children's cache entries (exactly as before) and every remaining key accumulates into the root's entry (stored under the reserved key) as a dict. Each consumer is dispatched at its own ratio tick with hold-last semantics identical to children.
  • Info / render. These channels nest by node name for children, so the root's entries are keyed by the root's own name (the reserved key is only used for internal state/routing and aggregation).
  • get_node never resolves the reserved key (it is not a user-facing path); get_nodes_by_fn does traverse the root node.

set_next_action(
    world_state: WorldStateT, node_state: CombinedNodeStateT, action: CombinedDataT
) -> Tuple[WorldStateT, CombinedNodeStateT]

Route combined actions to child nodes (and the optional root node), respecting per-node control rates.

The incoming action is split by :meth:_split_child_actions (children only). When a root_node owns an action space and no single node is the direct-action passthrough provider, the keys that do not belong to any named child are the root's action keys: they accumulate into the root's cache entry (stored under the reserved key) as a dict. Every consumer (children and root) is then dispatched at its own ratio tick, and only once it has received at least one action (hold-last semantics, so a child-only step re-delivers the root's previous action at its tick and vice versa).

docs.title: DataTransformation
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Abstract transformation between two UniEnv data spaces.

Transformations are used by wrappers, storages, and batch views to adapt data while keeping enough metadata to derive the target space and, when supported, reconstruct the inverse transform.

Reassigning an attribute of a transformation increments the global DataTransformation._config_epoch (attributes whose name ends with _cache are exempt), so caches derived from a transformation's configuration (e.g. ChainedTransformation's intermediate spaces) are rebuilt. Containers and arrays held by a transformation should be replaced, not mutated in place, once it has been used.

docs.title: Env
docs.text:
Bases: ABC, Generic[BArrayType, ContextType, ObsType, ActType, RenderFrame, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Stateful environment interface used throughout UniEnv.

An Env exposes typed action, observation, and optional context spaces plus the standard reset/step/render lifecycle. Concrete implementations may be single-instance or batched depending on batch_size.

docs.title: Batched-environment space invariant
docs.text:
The observation_space, action_space, and context_space (when present) always describe the data that the environment actually returns and accepts – including any batch dimension.

  • batch_size is None → the environment is unbatched. The spaces describe single-instance values (no leading batch axis).
  • batch_size == N (including N == 1) → the environment is batched with a leading batch dimension of size N. The spaces already include that leading batch dimension. Callers, wrappers, and downstream code must not apply an additional batch_space (or equivalent) on top of these spaces – doing so would double-batch and produce incorrect shapes.

This invariant matters whenever code builds source/target spaces from the env (e.g. replay-buffer builders, data transformations, or wrappers that unbatch per-slot data): always use the env-side spaces as-is and only unbatch/slice the data, never re-batch the space.

Bases: Env[BArrayType, ContextType, ObsType, ActType, RenderFrame, BDeviceType, BDtypeType, BRNGType]

Run multiple non-batched environments in separate worker processes.

Seeding follows :class:SyncVecEnv: reset(seed=s) resets worker i with seed s + i. If a worker raises, the exception is re-raised in the parent as a RuntimeError (chained to the worker's exception) and that worker process exits.

No environment is built in the parent process: the spaces, backend, device, metadata and render settings are reported by the workers (spaces travel as :func:space_to_json payloads, so this works with every start method), and the constructor raises if a worker fails to build its environment or if the workers disagree on backend or device. Differing sub-environment spaces are batched like in :class:SyncVecEnv.

Shared memory (shared_memory=True, the default): the parent allocates one buffer of shape (num_envs, *leaf_shape) per leaf of the single-env observation, context and action spaces. Worker i writes its observation / context into row i and reads its action from row i (step writes the whole action batch once and sends a payload-free command), so only reward, termination flags and info travel through the pipe and nothing is pickled or concatenated. Each group (observation, context, action) that cannot be shared falls back to the pipe on its own, with one INFO message on the unienv_interface.env_base.vec_env logger; :attr:shared_groups lists the groups that are shared. shared_memory=False sends everything through the pipe. Where the buffers live follows the worker env:

================ =============================== ================================= worker env buffer parent read ================ =============================== ================================= numpy host shared memory zero-copy numpy view torch CPU host shared memory zero-copy torch view torch CUDA CUDA buffer owned by the zero-copy on the GPU parent, shared via CUDA IPC jax CPU host shared memory copy=True: one copy into a fresh jax array; copy=False: zero-copy via DLPack (falls back to a copy if XLA refuses) jax GPU the same CUDA IPC buffer, with zero-copy via DLPack torch as carrier (DLPack in/out) jax TPU / other host shared memory (the worker one host-to-device transfer per devices copies device -> host) read ================ =============================== =================================

Actions use the same buffers in the other direction; every worker hands its env a private copy of its row.

Details of shared mode:

  • Only fixed-size spaces can be shared: BoxSpace / BinarySpace leaves nested in DictSpace / TupleSpace (other groups use the pipe). Observations and contexts must match their declared space exactly (shape and dtype per leaf); a mismatch raises in the worker and surfaces as the usual chained RuntimeError naming the leaf, nothing is cast silently (fix the env or pass shared_memory=False). Actions must have shape (num_envs, *action_leaf_shape); their dtype is cast with same-kind rules (e.g. float64 policy outputs into a float32 space). info always travels through the pipe.
  • copy=True (default) returns data that never changes afterwards. copy=False returns the shared buffers themselves (or zero-copy views of them): they are only valid until the next step / reset (which overwrite them in place) and must not be written to; copy anything you want to keep, and make sure asynchronous consumers (e.g. JAX computations) have finished before the next call. CUDA buffers are synchronised by the parent before every step / reset. Masked resets always return freshly gathered rows.
  • Every start method works. With fork (the Linux default) CUDA IPC works as long as the parent had not initialised CUDA before the workers were forked (no env is built in the parent, so that is the usual case); otherwise the workers cannot use CUDA at all, which torch reports when they build their env - use spawn / forkserver then. CUDA IPC is Linux-only; elsewhere CUDA buffers are staged through host shared memory (with a warning). JAX GPU envs need PyTorch as the IPC carrier and a CUDA-enabled jaxlib in the parent (otherwise they use the pipe). A TPU belongs to a single process, so TPU envs cannot be shared: run the workers on the host (or let them copy to the host) and the parent performs one host-to-TPU transfer per read.
  • Workers set XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false unless the variable is already set, so that N JAX workers do not each reserve 75% of the GPU.
  • The parent owns the buffers until :meth:close, which first shuts the workers down; host shared memory is unlinked on close (also after a worker crash) and when the env is garbage collected, and shared-memory envs that are still open at interpreter exit are closed then. Views returned with copy=False stay readable after close (the mapping is released with the last view). A worker that is killed hard (e.g. SIGKILL) cannot release its CUDA IPC references, in which case torch may warn about it when the parent exits.

Spawn worker processes and batch the spaces they report.

Recursively stack per-environment data into a batched backend representation.

  • A mapping is processed value by value.
  • A sequence of mappings that share the same keys (e.g. one info dict per sub-environment) becomes a mapping of stacked values.
  • A sequence of arrays or Python numbers is stacked into one array.
  • Strings, bytes and other objects are kept as a list.

By default the wrapper exposes the wrapped env's action_space, observation_space, and context_space unchanged. Never wrap an already-batched env space in an additional batch_space call.

docs.title: Space-forwarding invariant
docs.text:
By default the wrapper forwards the wrapped FuncEnv's action_space, observation_space, and context_space unchanged. Because the :class:FuncEnv contract guarantees that these spaces already include the batch dimension when the env is batched, subclasses that override a space must ensure the replacement still matches the batching status of the underlying env. Never wrap an already-batched env space in an additional batch_space call.

Wrap a functional environment and optionally override its interface metadata.

docs.title: unienv_interface.remote
docs.text:
Lightweight RPC for UniEnv environments, worlds, nodes and data transformations.

Host objects with :class:RemoteServer and use them through :class:RemoteClient proxies that implement the normal Env / World / WorldNode / DataTransformation interfaces. Transports: TCP, Unix sockets, WebSocket (optional websockets dependency) and in-memory. See docs/guides/remote-execution.md.

Modules:

A connection to a :class:RemoteServer. Thread-safe: calls may be concurrent.

Results are converted to backend arrays on device. A remote exception is re-raised as :class:RemoteError; a lost connection raises ConnectionError, in which case a call that was in flight may or may not have run on the server. timeout (seconds, None = wait forever) bounds each call; a timed-out call keeps running on the server.

docs.title: RemoteServer
docs.text:
RemoteServer(*, max_frame_size: int = DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_SIZE)

Serve registered objects to :class:RemoteClient connections.

Example::

with RemoteServer() as server:
    server.register("sim", env)  # or register_recursive() to also host its world and nodes
    server.serve("tcp://0.0.0.0:7000")  # blocks; or listen() in the background

Each registered root runs on its own worker thread, shared by every hosted object with the same world; calls on them are executed there one at a time, in arrival order, whichever client sent them. Only the methods in protocol.METHODS can be called.

Methods:

Name Description register

Host obj (an Env, World, WorldNode or DataTransformation) under name.

register_recursive

Like :meth:register, but also expose everything obj is built from.

Accept connections on address in the background; return the bound address.

serve

Listen on address and block until :meth:close (or Ctrl-C).

connect

An in-process client over a :class:MemoryTransport (mainly for tests).

close

Stop listening, drop every connection, close owned objects on their workers.

docs.title: register
docs.text:
register(
    name: str,
    obj: Hosted,
    *,
    close: bool = True,
    backend: Optional[ComputeBackend] = None,
    device: Optional[Any] = None,
) -> str

Host obj (an Env, World, WorldNode or DataTransformation) under name.

Only obj itself is exposed; use :meth:register_recursive to also expose the world and nodes it is built from. Objects sharing a world (e.g. an env and its world registered separately) run on the same worker. Registering an object that is already hosted returns its existing name. With close=True the server closes obj (on its worker) when it shuts down.

A DataTransformation has no backend of its own: backend / device (default: numpy, no device) are where the source spaces and data of its calls are rebuilt on the server. Other objects use their own.

An env built on a WorldEnv also exposes name/world and name/node (the root node), and every node exposes its world (<node name>/world, unless already hosted) and its children as <node name>/<child>, so clients can compose them in components mode. Objects already hosted keep their first name.

docs.title: unienv_interface.remote.compression
docs.text:
Opt-in lossy compression of server-to-client image arrays.

A client asks for it in hello, e.g. RemoteClient.connect(address, compress={"image": "jpeg:90"}). The server then encodes the uint8 leaves of results whose space has metadata["kind"] == "image" (layout "HWC" or "CHW", 1 or 3 channels; leading dimensions are batch dimensions) with that codec. Depth maps, float arrays and everything the client sends stay raw.

Codecs are pluggable (:func:unienv_interface.remote.wire.register_codec); the built-in jpeg codec uses OpenCV when installed, otherwise Pillow.

docs.title: unienv_interface.remote.proxies
docs.text:
Local Env / World / WorldNode / DataTransformation views of objects hosted by a server.

Every method is one remote call. Spaces, timings and metadata come from the server's descriptor; spaces are refreshed whenever a reset changed them. close() on a proxy does nothing: hosted objects belong to the server.

Components mode is a plain local WorldEnv over remote proxies (host them with server.register_recursive("sim", env))::

env = WorldEnv(client.world("sim/world"), client.node("sim/node"))

Serve registered objects to :class:RemoteClient connections.

Example::

with RemoteServer() as server:
    server.register("sim", env)  # or register_recursive() to also host its world and nodes
    server.serve("tcp://0.0.0.0:7000")  # blocks; or listen() in the background

docs.title: unienv_interface.remote.wire
docs.text:
Safe wire format: one JSON document plus raw binary attachments. No pickle.

A frame is::

u32 buffer count | u32 JSON length | u64 length per buffer | UTF-8 JSON | buffers...

(all little-endian). Plain JSON carries None, bools, ints, strings, lists and string-keyed dicts. Everything else is a JSON object tagged with the reserved key "__t":

========== =========================================================== ====================== tag fields decodes to ========== =========================================================== ====================== tuple v: list of values tuple dict v: list of [key, value] pairs dict (any hashable keys, or one using "__t" as a key) float v: "nan", "inf" or "-inf" non-finite float bytes b: buffer index bytes nd d: dtype string, s: shape, b: buffer index; array of the receiver's or c: codec, o: codec options, b: index list backend and device space v: space_to_json document Space graph v: dict of the GraphInstance fields GraphInstance ========== =========================================================== ======================

NumPy scalars travel as 0-d arrays; torch / JAX arrays are sent as NumPy arrays. Anything else raises TypeError: no arbitrary objects are ever reconstructed. Decoding validates every frame (sizes, buffer references, dtype allowlist, shape x itemsize == length, nesting depth) and raises WireError otherwise.

Bases: ABC, Generic[SpaceDataT, _SpaceBDeviceT, _SpaceBDTypeT, _SpaceBDRNGT]

Abstract description of a valid data domain.

Spaces carry backend, device, shape, and dtype metadata and define the operations needed by the rest of UniEnv: validation, sampling, empty value creation, serialization-friendly representation, and backend/device conversion for both the space definition and its data.

In-place changes to a space (reassigning one of its attributes, or e.g. DictSpace.__setitem__) increment the global Space._mutation_epoch. Caches keyed on a space's identity (e.g. in ChainedTransformation) include this counter, so mutating a space can never make them stale. BoxSpace is immutable after construction and is not tracked.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Every space carries an optional, read-only metadata mapping (constructor keyword metadata=) describing what its data means, e.g. BoxSpace(..., shape=(480, 640, 3), metadata={"kind": "image", "format": "rgb"}). Values must be JSON-serializable; they are validated and deep-copied at construction and exposed as a :class:SpaceMetadata (empty when absent). Nested spaces carry their own metadata, so every camera of a DictSpace observation can be described separately. Use :meth:with_metadata to get a copy of a space with other metadata.

Metadata is a description, not part of the data domain: __eq__, is_subspace and is_subspaceeq ignore it (use space_utils.metadata_utils.spaces_equal_with_metadata to compare it too). It is kept by to(), the batching utilities, serialization and the transformations that keep the meaning of the data, and dropped where the meaning is lost (e.g. flatten_space).

The keys below form a shared vocabulary understood by UniEnv utilities (e.g. the video wrappers and unienv_data.storages.dict_storage_kwargs_from_space). None of them is required or enforced at construction, and any other keys (and kinds) are allowed. "Per element" lists have one entry per element of the space's last axis:

  • kind (str): what the data is. Recommended: "image", "depth", "segmentation", "normal", "pointcloud", "proprio", "action", "pose", "force", "tactile", "teleop", "keypoints", "mask", "intrinsics", "extrinsics", "privileged", "task" (goals / targets), "state".
  • format (str): pixel format of images, "rgb", "bgr", "rgba", "bgra" or "gray".
  • layout (str): axis order of the trailing image dims, "HWC", "CHW" or "HW" (single channel without a channel axis); leading dims are batch dims.
  • units (str, or per element list of str): physical units, e.g. "m", "mm", "rad", "rad/s", "m/s", "m/s^2", "N", "N*m", "A", "V", "degC", "px", "s"; "normalized" for unitless normalized data.
  • frame (str): reference frame, e.g. "world", "base", "camera_cv" (OpenCV: x right, y down, z forward), "camera_gl", "link_local", "wrist".
  • rotation (str): rotation representation inside a pose / action vector, "quat_wxyz", "quat_xyzw", "euler_<axes>" with transforms3d axes (s static / extrinsic, r rotating / intrinsic, e.g. "euler_sxyz", "euler_rxyz"), "rot6d", "matrix" or "axis_angle".
  • control (str, actions): what is commanded, e.g. "joint_position", "joint_velocity", "joint_torque", "eef_pose", "eef_velocity", "gripper".
  • mode (str, actions): "absolute", "delta" or "velocity".
  • normalized (bool): the values are normalized.
  • range ([low, high], scalars or per element lists): the physical range normalized values map to, when known.
  • names (per element list of str): e.g. joint names.
  • source (str): name of the camera / sensor producing the data.
  • fps (positive number): capture rate of the source.
  • label (str): human readable name.

A vector packing several quantities (e.g. position 3 + quaternion 4 + gripper 1) is described per element with names and / or a units list, while rotation names the representation of its rotation part. space_utils.metadata_utils has builders for these keys (image_metadata, action_metadata, ...), annotate to attach metadata to nested spaces and validate_metadata to check it.

docs.title: is_subspaceeq
docs.text:
is_subspaceeq(other: Space) -> bool

Return whether this space is a non-strict subspace of other (self ⊆ other).

A space a is a non-strict subspace of b (a ⊆ b) when every valid sample of a is also a valid member of b; equality is allowed, i.e. a == b implies a.is_subspaceeq(b).

The primary use case is a controller that declares its REQUIRED observation space and checks required.is_subspaceeq(env_observation_space): for DictSpace this must hold even when the environment space exposes EXTRA keys beyond the required ones (unlike DictSpace.contains, which demands exact key equality). Controller-required-space checks should typically use is_subspaceeq rather than the strict is_subspace because a controller's required space may exactly equal the env space.

Comparison policy (structural only):

  • The two spaces must share the same backend type.
  • Dtypes must be strictly equal; no implicit cast widening is performed.
  • device is intentionally ignored — two spaces on different devices may still be in a subspace relation.

Cross-type comparisons (e.g. BoxSpace vs DictSpace) return False rather than raising. Subclasses override this method to provide concrete structural containment checks; the base implementation raises NotImplementedError to mirror the abstract-method style of this class.

docs.title: is_subspace
docs.text:
is_subspace(other: Space) -> bool

Return whether this space is a STRICT subspace of other (self ⊂ other).

Defined uniformly for all spaces as::

self.is_subspace(other)  ⟺  self.is_subspaceeq(other) and not other.is_subspaceeq(self)

I.e. self ⊆ other holds but other ⊆ self does not, so self is a PROPER (strict) subspace of other. This is the ⊂ relation versus the non-strict ⊆ provided by :meth:is_subspaceeq.

This definition is used instead of relying on __eq__ because some space classes only have identity __eq__; defining strict containment via the symmetric non-strict check works uniformly for all classes regardless of their __eq__ implementation.

For structurally-distinct-but-mutually-containing spaces (which should not occur under the strict dtype/shape policies enforced by the per-class is_subspaceeq implementations) this degrades gracefully to False: if both self.is_subspaceeq(other) and other.is_subspaceeq(self) hold, the two spaces are considered equivalent and neither is a STRICT subspace of the other.

If either side's is_subspaceeq is not implemented (the base :meth:is_subspaceeq raises NotImplementedError), the exception propagates to the caller — it is NOT swallowed into False so that callers can tell that the comparison is unsupported.

Note: controller-required-space checks should typically use :meth:is_subspaceeq (a controller's required space may exactly equal the env space, in which case the strict is_subspace would return False).

docs.title: clip
docs.text:
clip(x: Any) -> SpaceDataT

Project x onto this space and return the projected value.

clip is defined on the TARGET (subset) space. Contract: if self.is_subspaceeq(source) holds, then for every x with source.contains(x)::

self.contains(self.clip(x))

unless no meaningful projection exists, in which case clip raises ValueError instead of inventing data (e.g. a required DictSpace key is missing, or a string / dynamic axis / graph is shorter or smaller than this space's minimum; each space documents its cases).

Additionally:

  • clip is idempotent on members: self.clip(y) equals y whenever self.contains(y).
  • The input is never mutated; the result is new data, or x (or parts of it) itself where nothing needs to change.
  • The result follows this space's backend and dtype conventions (e.g. a BoxSpace casts to its dtype).

Inputs that are not members of any superspace (wrong structure, wrong shape, ...) are not supported and may raise.

The base implementation raises NotImplementedError to mirror the abstract-method style of this class; subclasses override it.

is_subspace(other: Space) -> bool

Return whether this space is a STRICT subspace of other (self ⊂ other).

Defined uniformly for all spaces as::

self.is_subspace(other)  ⟺  self.is_subspaceeq(other) and not other.is_subspaceeq(self)

I.e. self ⊆ other holds but other ⊆ self does not, so self is a PROPER (strict) subspace of other. This is the ⊂ relation versus the non-strict ⊆ provided by :meth:is_subspaceeq.

This definition is used instead of relying on __eq__ because some space classes only have identity __eq__; defining strict containment via the symmetric non-strict check works uniformly for all classes regardless of their __eq__ implementation.

For structurally-distinct-but-mutually-containing spaces (which should not occur under the strict dtype/shape policies enforced by the per-class is_subspaceeq implementations) this degrades gracefully to False: if both self.is_subspaceeq(other) and other.is_subspaceeq(self) hold, the two spaces are considered equivalent and neither is a STRICT subspace of the other.

If either side's is_subspaceeq is not implemented (the base :meth:is_subspaceeq raises NotImplementedError), the exception propagates to the caller — it is NOT swallowed into False so that callers can tell that the comparison is unsupported.

Note: controller-required-space checks should typically use :meth:is_subspaceeq (a controller's required space may exactly equal the env space, in which case the strict is_subspace would return False).
