docs.title: Design Direction
docs.text:
UniEnv keeps two ideas front and center:

  • Structure should stay explicit. Observations, actions, contexts, and stored transitions should remain described by spaces instead of becoming anonymous tensors too early.
  • Backend choice should stay late. The same logic should be able to target NumPy, PyTorch, JAX, and storage-layer backends with minimal translation code.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
UniEnv exposes two environment styles:

  • Env: a stateful object that owns its runtime state internally
  • FuncEnv: a functional interface that passes state explicitly

Both carry the same high-level contract: typed action, observation, and optional context spaces plus the standard reset, step, and render lifecycle.

docs.title: Env
docs.text:
Use Env when you want the familiar environment shape:

  • reset(...) -> context, observation, info
  • step(action) -> observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info
  • render()

This is the most direct fit for interactive control loops, evaluation harnesses, and compatibility layers that expect a stateful object.

Important properties exposed by Env implementations:

  • action_space
  • observation_space
  • context_space
  • backend
  • device
  • batch_size

Env also includes convenience helpers such as sample_action() and sample_observation(), which draw from the declared spaces while updating the environment RNG.

docs.title: FuncEnv
docs.text:
Use FuncEnv when explicit state passing is more important than object-owned mutable state.

The core methods are:

  • initial(...) -> state, context, observation, info
  • reset(state, ...) -> state, context, observation, info
  • step(state, action) -> state, observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info

This style is useful when you want:

  • JAX-friendly execution patterns
  • easier functional composition
  • tighter control over state snapshots, rollouts, or transformations

docs.title: Bridging The Two
docs.text:
FuncEnvBasedEnv adapts a FuncEnv into a stateful Env.

That means you can:

  • implement the hard logic once in functional form
  • expose a familiar object-oriented environment API to downstream code
  • keep wrappers and tooling that expect Env unchanged

docs.title: Batched Environments
docs.text:
Both environment styles can represent batched execution through batch_size.

When batch_size is set:

  • actions, observations, rewards, and done flags are expected to carry a batch dimension
  • reset(mask=...) can reset only selected batch elements
  • helper methods such as update_observation_post_reset merge masked resets back into a full batch

docs.title: Space invariant for batched environments
docs.text:
A key contract that all Env and FuncEnv implementations share:

If an environment is batched, then its observation_space, action_space, and context_space (when present) already describe batched values.

Concretely:

batch_size Meaning Spaces None Unbatched – single instance, no leading batch axis. Describe single-instance values. N (including 1) Batched – leading batch dimension of size N. Already include the leading batch axis of size N.

batch_size == 1 is still a batched environment. Its spaces carry a leading dimension of size 1; they are not the same as the unbatched spaces.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Code that builds source/target spaces from the env – replay-buffer builders, data transformations, wrappers that unbatch per-slot data – must use the env-side spaces as-is. Applying an additional batch_space(...) on top of an already-batched env space will double-batch and produce incorrect shapes.

Common patterns:

  • Correct: source_space = env.observation_space (works for both batched and unbatched envs).
  • Incorrect: source_space = batch_space(env.observation_space, env.batch_size) when the env is already batched – this adds a second batch dimension.
  • Unbatching per-slot data: use get_at(env.observation_space, data, i) to slice slot i out of the batched data; the resulting per-slot space is the single-instance space obtained by unbatching env.observation_space, not by re-batching it.

docs.title: Wrappers
docs.text:
UniEnv wrappers work at the Env layer. They can change:

  • the action interface
  • the observation and context interface
  • backend placement
  • episode length
  • rendering and video export behavior

See Wrappers and Transformations for the main wrapper stack.

docs.title: When To Use Which
docs.text:
Choose Env if:

  • you want the most familiar interface
  • your simulator already manages mutable runtime state
  • you are wrapping an existing imperative system

Choose FuncEnv if:

  • you want explicit state passing
  • you care about purely functional rollout logic
  • you want the same core logic to be easier to test, checkpoint, or stage

Use FuncEnvBasedEnv if you want both.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
unienv_policy is the agent side of the loop. Like environments, policies come in two styles:

  • Policy: a stateful object that keeps its own memory (RNG, recurrent state, history)
  • FuncPolicy: a functional interface that takes its state in and returns it explicitly

A policy declares the same kind of spaces an environment does (observation_space, action_space, optional context_space, plus backend, device and batch_size), so it can be checked against, and written for, any environment with matching spaces: a simulator, a real robot, or a dataset replayed through the same schema.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
Subclass Policy and implement compute_action. The other methods have do-nothing defaults:

Method Called Default reset(context, observation, *, seed=None, mask=None) after env.reset; with mask, only the masked batch entries were reset no-op compute_action(observation) every step required observe_transition(action_taken, new_observation) after env.step, for policies that track history no-op visualize_action(environment_render, observation, action) to draw the action on a render frame returns the frame close() when done no-op

sample_action(), sample_observation() and sample_context() draw from the declared spaces and advance policy.rng.

import numpy as np

from unienv_interface.backends.numpy import NumpyComputeBackend as B
from unienv_interface.space import BoxSpace
from unienv_policy import Policy

obs_space = BoxSpace(B, -10.0, 10.0, np.float32, shape=(3,))
act_space = BoxSpace(B, -1.0, 1.0, np.float32, shape=(2,))


class RandomPolicy(Policy):
    """Uniform random actions from the action space."""

    def __init__(self, observation_space, action_space, seed=0):
        self.backend = observation_space.backend
        self.device = observation_space.device
        self.observation_space = observation_space
        self.action_space = action_space
        self.rng = self.backend.random.random_number_generator(seed)

    def compute_action(self, observation, **kwargs):
        return self.sample_action()


policy = RandomPolicy(obs_space, act_space)
policy.compute_action(np.zeros(3, np.float32))  # array of shape (2,), within [-1, 1]

In a real setup, pass env.observation_space and env.action_space, so the policy is built from the environment it runs in.

docs.title: The Control Loop
docs.text:
The same loop drives a policy against any Env:

context, obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)
policy.reset(context, obs, seed=0)
for _ in range(100):
    action = policy.compute_action(obs)
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)
    policy.observe_transition(action, obs)

With a batched environment, reset only the finished entries: env.reset(mask=done) returns their context and observation, and policy.reset(context, obs, mask=done) resets the same entries.

docs.title: FuncPolicy
docs.text:
A FuncPolicy keeps no state on the object. Each method takes the state and returns the next one, which fits jax.jit, vectorized rollouts, and checkpointing:

  • initial(context, observation, *, batch_size, seed=None) -> state (required)
  • compute_action(state, observation) -> (state, action) (required)
  • reset(state, context, observation, *, seed=None, mask=None) -> state
  • observe_transition(state, action_taken, new_observation) -> state
  • close(state)
from unienv_policy import FuncPolicy


class SmoothedPolicy(FuncPolicy):
    """Moves the action a fraction of the way toward a target each step; the state is the last action."""

    def __init__(self, observation_space, action_space, alpha=0.5):
        self.backend = observation_space.backend
        self.device = observation_space.device
        self.observation_space = observation_space
        self.action_space = action_space
        self.alpha = alpha

    def initial(self, context, observation, *, batch_size, seed=None, **kwargs):
        return np.zeros(2, np.float32)

    def compute_action(self, state, observation, **kwargs):
        target = np.clip(observation[:2], -1.0, 1.0)
        action = state + self.alpha * (target - state)
        return action, action


func_policy = SmoothedPolicy(obs_space, act_space)
obs = np.array([1.0, -1.0, 0.0], np.float32)
state = func_policy.initial(None, obs, batch_size=None)
state, action = func_policy.compute_action(state, obs)  # [0.5, -0.5]
state, action = func_policy.compute_action(state, obs)  # [0.75, -0.75]

docs.title: Running A FuncPolicy As A Policy
docs.text:
FuncPolicyBasedPolicy holds the state for you, so a functional policy plugs into the stateful loop above:

from unienv_policy import FuncPolicyBasedPolicy

policy = FuncPolicyBasedPolicy(func_policy, seed=0)
policy.reset(None, obs)          # calls func_policy.initial the first time
policy.compute_action(obs)       # [0.5, -0.5]

docs.title: Wrappers
docs.text:
PolicyWrapper and FuncPolicyWrapper forward every call and attribute to the wrapped policy, the same way environment wrappers do. Override only what you change:

from unienv_policy import PolicyWrapper


class ScaledActions(PolicyWrapper):
    def __init__(self, policy, scale):
        super().__init__(policy)
        self.scale = scale

    def compute_action(self, observation, **kwargs):
        return self.scale * self.policy.compute_action(observation, **kwargs)


slow = ScaledActions(FuncPolicyBasedPolicy(SmoothedPolicy(obs_space, act_space)), 0.5)
slow.reset(None, obs)
slow.compute_action(obs)         # [0.25, -0.25]
slow.unwrapped                   # the FuncPolicyBasedPolicy underneath

unwrapped, prev_wrapper_layer and get_wrapper_attr / set_wrapper_attr walk the wrapper stack.

docs.title: Spaces And Backends
docs.text:
Space is the core data contract in UniEnv.

A space does more than describe shape:

  • it declares what values are valid
  • it knows which backend and device the data belongs to
  • it can sample data
  • it can create empty values
  • it can convert both the space definition and concrete data across backends

docs.title: Why Spaces Matter
docs.text:
The rest of the package depends on spaces:

  • environments expose action_space, observation_space, and context_space
  • wrappers transform spaces when they transform runtime data
  • replay buffers and storages know what one sample should look like
  • flattening, batching, serialization, and validation all start from the space definition

docs.title: Main Space Types
docs.text:
The most important built-in spaces are:

  • BoxSpace: continuous or integer tensor-like ranges
  • BinarySpace: boolean tensors
  • DictSpace: named structured collections of subspaces
  • TupleSpace: positional structured collections
  • TextSpace: string-valued data
  • GraphSpace: graph-structured data
  • UnionSpace: one-of-many alternatives
  • BatchedSpace: a batched view over another space
  • DynamicBoxSpace: shape or bounds that are determined dynamically

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
Each space is tied to a ComputeBackend, such as:

  • NumPy
  • PyTorch
  • JAX

Because the backend is part of the space definition, UniEnv can move both metadata and data in a consistent way:

target_space = source_space.to(target_backend, target_device)
target_data = source_space.data_to(data, target_backend, target_device)

This is the mechanism used by backend-conversion wrappers and many data utilities.

docs.title: Structured Data Without Losing Structure
docs.text:
UniEnv does not force you to flatten observations or actions at the boundary.

You can keep rich structures such as:

  • nested dictionaries for multi-sensor observations
  • separate action components for different effectors
  • mixed image, state, and text metadata in one sample

When a downstream system needs dense arrays, use the helpers in:

  • unienv_interface.space.space_utils.flatten_utils
  • unienv_interface.space.space_utils.batch_utils

Those utilities are also used internally by wrappers, batches, and replay buffers.

docs.title: Subspaces And Clipping
docs.text:
a.is_subspaceeq(b) checks a ⊆ b: every valid value of a is also valid in b (equality allowed). a.is_subspace(b) is the strict a ⊂ b. The check is structural: same space type, backend and dtype, with tighter bounds, shape / length / count ranges or charsets, and for DictSpace a subset of the keys. A controller can therefore declare the observation space it requires and check it with required.is_subspaceeq(env.observation_space), even when the environment exposes extra keys.

clip goes the other way. Called on the subspace, it projects any value of the larger space onto it:

if required.is_subspaceeq(env.observation_space):
    obs = required.clip(env_obs)   # required.contains(obs) holds

clip leaves values that already belong to the space unchanged, never modifies its input, and returns data with the space's backend and dtype. When a value cannot be projected without inventing data, clip raises ValueError:

Space clip ValueError when BoxSpace clamps to the bounds (±inf bounds keep values), casts to the box dtype never BinarySpace returns the value (only an identical space is a subspace) never DynamicBoxSpace trims axes longer than shape_high, clamps the values an axis is shorter than shape_low DictSpace drops extra keys, clips each value a key of the space is missing TupleSpace / BatchedSpace clips each element an element cannot be clipped UnionSpace clips the value with the alternative at the same index the value cannot be clipped TextSpace removes characters outside the charset, truncates to max_length fewer than min_length characters remain GraphSpace keeps the first max_nodes nodes (dropping their edges), then the first max_edges edges, clamps the features; per graph in a batch fewer than min_nodes nodes or min_edges edges remain

docs.title: Space Metadata
docs.text:
Shape, dtype and bounds say what values are valid, not what they mean. Every space therefore takes an optional, read-only metadata mapping of JSON values:

from unienv_interface.space import BoxSpace, DictSpace

obs_space = DictSpace(backend, {
    "front": BoxSpace(backend, 0, 255, np.uint8, shape=(3, 480, 640),
                      metadata={"kind": "image", "format": "rgb", "layout": "CHW", "source": "front_cam", "fps": 30}),
    "joints": BoxSpace(backend, -3.14, 3.14, np.float32, shape=(7,),
                       metadata={"kind": "proprio", "units": "rad"}),
})

obs_space["front"].metadata["layout"]         # "CHW"
wrist = obs_space["front"].with_metadata(source="wrist_cam")  # a new space; the original is unchanged

Nested spaces carry their own metadata, so each camera in a DictSpace is described separately. The keys below form a shared vocabulary. None is required and none is enforced when a space is built; any other keys (and kinds) are allowed. "Per element" means a list with one entry per element of the space's last axis.

Key Type Meaning Values / examples kind str what the data is recommended: "image", "depth", "segmentation", "normal", "pointcloud", "proprio", "action", "pose", "force", "tactile", "teleop", "keypoints", "mask", "intrinsics", "extrinsics", "privileged", "task" (goals / targets), "state"; others allowed format str pixel format of an image "rgb", "bgr", "rgba", "bgra", "gray" layout str axis order of the trailing image dims (leading dims are batch dims) "HWC", "CHW", "HW" (single channel, no channel axis) units str, or per element list of str physical units "m", "mm", "rad", "rad/s", "m/s", "m/s^2", "N", "N*m", "A", "V", "degC", "px", "s"; "normalized" for unitless normalized data frame str reference frame "world", "base", "camera_cv" (OpenCV: x right, y down, z forward), "camera_gl", "link_local", "wrist" rotation str rotation representation inside a pose / action vector "quat_wxyz", "quat_xyzw", "euler_<axes>" with transforms3d axes (s static / extrinsic, r rotating / intrinsic, e.g. "euler_sxyz", "euler_rxyz"), "rot6d", "matrix", "axis_angle" control str what an action commands "joint_position", "joint_velocity", "joint_torque", "eef_pose", "eef_velocity", "gripper" mode str how an action commands it "absolute", "delta", "velocity" normalized bool the values are normalized True range [low, high], scalars or per element lists the physical range normalized values map to, when known [-0.05, 0.05], [[-3.14, -2.0], [3.14, 2.0]] names per element list of str names of the elements ["shoulder", "elbow", "wrist"] source str camera or sensor name "front_cam" fps positive number capture rate 30 label str human readable name "gripper camera"

A vector that packs several quantities, e.g. an end-effector command of position (3) + quaternion (4) + gripper (1), is described per element with names and / or a units list, and rotation names the representation of its rotation part:

from unienv_interface.space.space_utils.metadata_utils import action_metadata

action_space = BoxSpace(backend, -1.0, 1.0, np.float32, shape=(8,), metadata=action_metadata(
    control="eef_pose", mode="delta", frame="base", rotation="quat_wxyz",
    names=["x", "y", "z", "qw", "qx", "qy", "qz", "gripper"],
    units=["m", "m", "m", "normalized", "normalized", "normalized", "normalized", "normalized"],
))

Metadata describes the data but is not part of the data domain: ==, is_subspace and is_subspaceeq ignore it, so compatibility checks between environments, wrappers and replay buffers are unaffected. Use space_utils.metadata_utils.spaces_equal_with_metadata to compare it too, and find_spaces_by_metadata(space, kind="image") to locate the described leaves.

Metadata follows the space where its meaning survives: space.to(...), the batching utilities, serialization, frame stacking and the transformations that keep the meaning of the data (rescale, crop, image resize, batchify, dict filtering and flattening). It is dropped where the meaning is lost, e.g. by flatten_space, and spaces built from data (construct_space_from_data, from_gym_space) have none.

When combined world nodes merge their children's spaces, a child's space nested under the child's name keeps its metadata, the dict a CombinedWorldNode merges its root node's keys into keeps the root's metadata, and the dict a FlatCombinedWorldNode merges several dicts into keeps their metadata only if all of them have the same.

UniEnv uses it to:

  • record the image leaves of observations with the video wrappers, converting CHW / bgr images for writing
  • route image leaves to image storages with dict_storage_kwargs_from_space
  • describe the features of LeRobot datasets

docs.title: Metadata Helpers
docs.text:
unienv_interface.space.space_utils.metadata_utils has helpers so that environments and adaptors describe their spaces the same way.

The builders return plain dicts with the vocabulary keys, dropping arguments left at None, so keys cannot be misspelled: image_metadata(*, format="rgb", layout="HWC", source=None, fps=None, **extra), depth_metadata(*, units="m", layout="HW", source=None, fps=None, **extra), proprio_metadata(*, units=None, names=None, frame=None, rotation=None, **extra), action_metadata(*, control=None, mode=None, units=None, normalized=None, range=None, names=None, frame=None, rotation=None, **extra) and, for any other kind, metadata(kind, **fields):

from unienv_interface.space.space_utils.metadata_utils import image_metadata, depth_metadata, metadata

camera_space = DictSpace(backend, {
    "rgb": BoxSpace(backend, 0, 255, np.uint8, shape=(480, 640, 3),
                    metadata=image_metadata(source="front_cam", fps=30)),
    "depth": BoxSpace(backend, 0.0, 10.0, np.float32, shape=(480, 640),
                      metadata=depth_metadata(source="front_cam", fps=30)),
    "intrinsics": BoxSpace(backend, -np.inf, np.inf, np.float32, shape=(3, 3),
                           metadata=metadata("intrinsics", source="front_cam")),
})

annotate(space, mapping, *, replace=False, strict=True) attaches metadata to an existing (e.g. converted or inferred) space. Each key of mapping is a path through nested DictSpace and TupleSpace spaces, a "/"-separated string or a tuple of dict keys and tuple positions, with "" / () for the space itself. Its metadata is merged into that space's (replaced with replace=True); everything else, including metadata already present, is kept. Unknown paths raise a KeyError listing all of them unless strict=False:

from unienv_interface.space.space_utils.gym_utils import from_gym_space
from unienv_interface.space.space_utils.metadata_utils import annotate, image_metadata, proprio_metadata

obs_space = annotate(from_gym_space(env.observation_space, backend), {
    "pixels": image_metadata(source="front_cam"),
    "agent/qpos": proprio_metadata(units="rad", names=joint_names),
    ("agent", "tcp_pose"): proprio_metadata(frame="base", rotation="quat_wxyz"),
})

metadata_issues(space) lists the problems with the metadata of a space and all its nested spaces, and validate_metadata(space) raises a ValueError listing them. They check the types of the vocabulary keys, the values of format, layout and rotation, that per element lists match the last axis of array spaces, and that image and depth spaces fit their layout and format (rgb / bgr 3 channels, rgba / bgra 4, gray 1, depth 1; leading batch dims allowed). They are lenient: unknown keys and kinds pass, and what cannot be checked is not. Use them in an adaptor's tests:

from unienv_interface.space.space_utils.metadata_utils import validate_metadata

def test_spaces_are_described():
    env = make_env()
    validate_metadata(env.observation_space)
    validate_metadata(env.action_space)

common_metadata(spaces) returns the metadata all spaces share (empty if they differ); it is the rule used where several spaces become one.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
Spaces can be serialized and restored through the space serialization helpers used across the package.

That matters when:

  • a replay buffer needs to persist its schema
  • a storage backend needs to reconstruct structured data on load
  • a transformation or wrapper needs to preserve its target-space definition

Serialized spaces include their (nested) metadata when there is any; payloads written before metadata existed still load.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
Use a DictSpace when the names of fields matter to downstream code.

Use a flattened representation only at the boundary where a learner, policy, or storage format truly needs it.

Keep the original structured space around as long as possible. That is where most of UniEnv's portability comes from.

docs.title: World Composition
docs.text:
UniEnv can build an environment from smaller pieces instead of forcing everything into one monolithic class.

The relevant abstractions are:

  • World: the shared simulator or runtime
  • WorldNode: one subsystem layered on top of that world
  • WorldEnv: an Env that composes a world and one or more nodes

docs.title: World
docs.text:
World owns the underlying runtime state.

Typical responsibilities:

  • stepping the simulator or real-time clock
  • resetting or reloading the runtime
  • exposing a backend, device, and optional batch size
  • coordinating timestep information

UniEnv includes RealWorld, which measures wall-clock elapsed time and is useful for real-time control loops.

docs.title: WorldNode
docs.text:
A WorldNode represents one logical concern inside the world, such as:

  • a robot controller
  • a sensor
  • a reward model
  • a termination rule
  • an object or scene component

Nodes expose some combination of:

  • action_space
  • observation_space
  • context_space
  • reward, termination, and truncation signals
  • rendering output

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
WorldEnv drives a staged lifecycle around the world and its nodes.

Reset flow:

  1. World.reset()
  2. node reset(...)
  3. World.after_reset()
  4. node after_reset(...)
  5. read context, observation, and info

Reload flow:

  1. World.reload()
  2. node reload(...)
  3. World.after_reload()
  4. node after_reload(...)
  5. read context, observation, and info

Step flow:

  1. node receives the next action
  2. node pre_environment_step(...)
  3. World.step()
  4. node post_environment_step(...)
  5. read observation, reward, done flags, and info

docs.title: Priorities
docs.text:
Nodes opt into lifecycle callbacks through priority sets such as:

  • reset_priorities
  • reload_priorities
  • after_reset_priorities
  • after_reload_priorities
  • pre_environment_step_priorities
  • post_environment_step_priorities

Higher priorities run earlier.

This lets you coordinate scene setup order, controller updates, reward computation, and sensor refreshes without hard-coding everything into one call site.

docs.title: Combined Nodes
docs.text:
If you pass multiple nodes to WorldEnv, UniEnv wraps them in a CombinedWorldNode.

That gives you:

  • one environment surface
  • aggregated spaces and signals
  • nested node lookup helpers such as get_node(...)

docs.title: When To Use World Composition
docs.text:
Use the world/node stack when:

  • your environment is naturally composed from reusable subsystems
  • you need clear ordering around scene construction and runtime updates
  • you want one simulator world to power multiple observation or control components

If your environment is simple and self-contained, a direct Env or FuncEnv can still be the better fit.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text: These guides cover the parts of UniEnv you are most likely to reach for after the core abstractions click.

docs.title: Dataset Integrations
docs.text:
UniEnv can wrap external dataset ecosystems behind the same BatchBase interface used by replay buffers and storages.

That means downstream code can often stay unchanged whether its data comes from:

  • a live replay buffer
  • a local dataset on disk
  • a Hugging Face dataset
  • a PyTorch Dataset

docs.title: Hugging Face Datasets
docs.text:
HFAsUniEnvDataset adapts a datasets.Dataset into a UniEnv batch.

Highlights:

  • infers a UniEnv space from the first sample
  • configures the Hugging Face dataset format to match the requested backend
  • supports column selection through the batch column-view helpers

Use it when your training or evaluation data is already managed through the Hugging Face datasets stack.

docs.title: LeRobot Datasets
docs.text:
LeRobotAsUniEnvDataset reads local or Hub-hosted LeRobot datasets without requiring the upstream lerobot Python package.

Highlights:

  • supports multiple LeRobot dataset versions
  • reconstructs a DictSpace from dataset features
  • can include or exclude named features
  • can optionally decode video features
  • describes the features through space metadata: image and video features carry {"kind": "image", "format": "rgb", "layout": "HWC", "fps": <dataset fps>, "source": <feature key>}, observation.state and action carry kind "proprio" / "action"

This is the most direct path for bringing LeRobot-formatted robotics datasets into UniEnv-native tooling.

docs.title: PyTorch Dataset Adapters
docs.text:
UniEnv provides both directions:

  • PyTorchAsUniEnvDataset: wrap an existing PyTorch Dataset as a UniEnv batch
  • UniEnvAsPyTorchDataset: expose a UniEnv batch as a PyTorch Dataset

This is useful when the training stack expects PyTorch dataloaders but the storage or replay layer is written against UniEnv.

docs.title: Choosing An Adapter
docs.text:
Use a UniEnv adapter when you want:

  • one indexing interface across multiple dataset sources
  • space-aware structured samples instead of ad hoc dictionaries
  • the ability to plug the result into UniEnv samplers or downstream wrappers

Use the original upstream dataset API directly when you need ecosystem-specific features that are outside the UniEnv batch contract.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: This page collects the maintenance workflow for UniEnvPy.

docs.title: Local Setup
docs.text:
From the UniEnvPy directory:

pip install -e .[dev,gymnasium,video]
pytest

Install backend- or integration-specific dependencies separately if you are working on those areas.

docs.title: Documentation Generation
docs.text:
The docs site combines:

  • hand-written pages under docs/
  • generated API pages created by docs/gen_ref_pages.py

The generation step walks the unienv_interface and unienv_data modules and emits reference pages consumed by mkdocstrings.

The look comes from the shared UniEnv docs theme, which lives in docs-theme/ of UniEnvOrg.github.io. Fetch it once, then serve:

pip install -e ".[docs]"
scripts/fetch_docs_theme.sh        # or: scripts/fetch_docs_theme.sh ../UniEnvOrg.github.io
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Published versions
docs.text:
The site is versioned with mike on the gh-pages branch, by the Deploy Docs workflow:

Trigger Published at push to main /UniEnv/dev/ GitHub release X /UniEnv/X/, also aliased as /UniEnv/latest/ (the default) manual run with a version that version, optionally made latest

Links from before versioning (/UniEnv/concepts/...) are redirected to the same page under latest/.

docs.title: What To Keep Stable
docs.text:
For release-facing docs, the most important guarantees to keep visible are:

  • the distinction between unienv_interface and unienv_data
  • the difference between Env and FuncEnv
  • the role of Space as the schema contract across runtime and storage code
  • the storage-backed nature of replay buffers
  • the world/node composition model for richer environments

docs.title: Before A Release
docs.text:
Check at least the following:

  1. README.md reflects the current package layout and installation story.
  2. The docs landing page matches the actual module boundaries.
  3. mkdocs build succeeds without broken references.
  4. Tests covering wrappers, spaces, transformations, and replay buffers still pass.

docs.title: Remote execution
docs.text:
unienv_interface.remote is a small RPC layer: a RemoteServer hosts existing Env, World, WorldNode and DataTransformation objects, and a RemoteClient returns proxies that implement the same interfaces. Each proxy method is one remote call.

Transports: TCP and Unix domain sockets (standard library), WebSocket (pip install 'unienv[network]'), and an in-memory pair for tests.

docs.title: Hosting an environment
docs.text:
from unienv_interface.remote import RemoteServer

with RemoteServer() as server:
    server.register("robot", make_env())     # an Env, World or WorldNode
    server.serve("tcp://0.0.0.0:7000")      # blocks until Ctrl-C

listen(address) starts the same listener in the background and returns the bound address (use port 0 for a free port). Addresses are tcp://host:port, unix:///path/to.sock or ws://host:port; a server can listen on several.

from unienv_interface.remote import RemoteClient

with RemoteClient.connect("tcp://robot-pc:7000") as client:
    env = client.env("robot")
    context, observation, info = env.reset(seed=42)
    observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(env.sample_action())

RemoteEnv has the hosted env's spaces, batch_size, render_mode, render_fps, metadata and timings. Results are converted to the client's backend and device (RemoteClient.connect(address, backend=PyTorchComputeBackend, device="cuda")); arguments are converted to the hosted object's backend and device on the server. server.connect() returns an in-process client (same wire format, no sockets).

The protocol has no authentication. Bind to loopback or a trusted network, or tunnel it (SSH, VPN).

docs.title: Hosting a data transformation
docs.text:
A DataTransformation can be served too, e.g. one whose dependencies live in another Python environment. It has no backend of its own: register it with the backend and device its calls should run on, and the source space and data of each call are rebuilt there.

from unienv_interface.backends.pytorch import PyTorchComputeBackend

server.register("grasps", make_transformation(), backend=PyTorchComputeBackend, device="cuda")

transformation = client.transformation("grasps")   # a RemoteDataTransformation
target_space = transformation.get_target_space_from_source(source_space)
result = transformation.transform(source_space, data)

Only transform and get_target_space_from_source are remote. The proxy has no inverse and cannot be serialized (it is bound to its connection): a storage that serializes its transformations needs the hosted one.

docs.title: Threads and concurrency
docs.text:
Every registered root object gets one worker thread. All calls on it, and on the world and nodes it exposes, run on that thread one at a time, in arrival order. Simulators that need thread affinity therefore always see the same thread. Any number of clients may connect and call; their calls simply queue. A client is thread-safe and may be shared by several threads. Different roots run in parallel.

When the server closes, it drops all connections and closes the objects registered with close=True (the default) on their worker threads. Proxies' close() does nothing: clients never close hosted objects.

docs.title: Errors, timeouts and disconnects
docs.text:
• An exception raised by the hosted object is re-raised as RemoteError, with the remote exception's class name (err.type), message and traceback (err.remote_traceback, also included in str(err)). The connection stays usable.
  • Only the methods of the standard interfaces can be called (reset, step, render, ... see unienv_interface.remote.protocol.METHODS); anything else is rejected. There is no generic attribute access.
  • If the connection is lost, every pending and later call raises ConnectionError. A call interrupted by a disconnect may or may not have run on the server: nothing is retried, so check the state (or reset) after reconnecting.
  • RemoteClient.connect(address, timeout=5.0) bounds every call; a timed-out call raises TimeoutError but keeps running on the server (the late reply is dropped).

docs.title: Spaces that change on reset
docs.text: Spaces are sent once, in the hello handshake. After each reset / reload / after_reset / after_reload, the server checks whether any space of that root (including its world's nodes) changed and, if so, attaches the new spaces to the next response for every client. Proxies update their observation_space, action_space and context_space in place.

docs.title: Components mode
docs.text:
server.register(name, obj) hosts only obj itself. To also host what an env is built from, use server.register_recursive(name, env): for an env built on a WorldEnv it exposes its world as <name>/world, its root node as <name>/node and every child node as <node name>/<child name> (for example robot/node/camera). You can also register individual worlds and nodes yourself with register; objects that share a world always run on the same worker. Compose them with a plain local WorldEnv (or a local combination of remote child nodes); each lifecycle hook is then one remote call:

from unienv_interface.world import WorldEnv

server.register_recursive("robot", make_env())   # on the server

world = client.world("robot/world")
env = WorldEnv(world, client.node("robot/node"))   # the whole node tree
env = WorldEnv(world, [client.node("robot/node/arm"), client.node("robot/node/camera")])

client.resources lists every hosted resource with its descriptor (kind, callable methods, and links to its world, root node and children when those are hosted too; a node proxy's world, nodes and get_node only see hosted objects). A node whose world is None runs on its own worker; it must declare backend / device for argument conversion.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
with observer.subscribe("robot") as stream:
    for event in stream:                    # or stream.next(timeout=1.0)
        print(event.kind, event.sequence, event.value)

A subscription yields the result of every reset, reload and step of a hosted env, whichever client called it, as SubscriptionEvent(kind, sequence, value). Delivery is latest-wins: a slow subscriber skips results (visible as gaps in sequence) and never slows the server or other clients down. Closing the subscription unsubscribes; a lost connection ends it with ConnectionError.

docs.title: Image compression
docs.text:
Over a slow network, a client can ask for lossy compression of camera images:

client = RemoteClient.connect(address, compress={"image": "jpeg:90"})  # quality 1-100

The server then JPEG-encodes every uint8 leaf of a reset / step result (and of node get_observation / get_context) whose space has metadata["kind"] == "image", laid out HWC or CHW (metadata["layout"], default HWC) with 1 or 3 channels (metadata["format"]: rgb, bgr or gray); leading dimensions are batch dimensions. Everything else (depth maps, float images, RGBA, arrays without image metadata) and everything the client sends stays raw. Each client chooses for itself; the default is raw. Encoding uses OpenCV when installed, otherwise Pillow.

An 84x84 RGB image shrinks about 11x and costs ~20 µs to encode plus ~20 µs to decode, so it pays off once the link is slower than a few hundred Mbit/s; on loopback raw is faster. Other codecs can be added with unienv_interface.remote.wire.register_codec (on both sides).

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Arrays travel as raw attachments next to a small JSON header, with no pickling and no copies on the sending side; stream sockets send each frame with one sendmsg. On one machine a step with a small observation takes about 40-50 µs over TCP or Unix sockets, an 84x84x3 image about 50 µs and a batch of 64 such images about 140-160 µs; WebSocket adds roughly 50 µs per call. Run python benchmarks/envs/bench_remote.py to measure your setup.

docs.title: Runnable examples
docs.text:
python examples/remote/environment.py
python examples/remote/components.py

See the protocol reference for the wire format.

docs.title: Replay Buffers And Storage
docs.text: unienv_data brings the same typed-space approach to stored data.

docs.title: BatchBase
docs.text:
BatchBase is the common interface for dataset-like collections of structured samples.

It gives you a uniform API for:

  • indexed reads
  • structured or flattened access
  • metadata-aware retrieval
  • column views and sliced views
  • extension from other batches

Because a batch knows the Space of one sample, UniEnv can keep structured data and flattened tensor views in sync.

docs.title: ReplayBuffer
docs.text:
ReplayBuffer is the main mutable buffer abstraction.

Key properties:

  • ring-buffer overwrite semantics
  • persistence metadata
  • pluggable backing storage
  • optional multiprocessing-safe counters and locking
  • step-wise append(value) with implicit segment starts
  • mark_segment_end() to finalize the current segment
  • get_segments() for ReplayBuffer-owned segment metadata, with a legacy fallback for old metadata

Typical creation pattern:

import numpy as np

from unienv_interface.backends.numpy import NumpyComputeBackend
from unienv_interface.space.spaces import BoxSpace, DictSpace
from unienv_data.replay_buffer import ReplayBuffer
from unienv_data.storages.parquet import ParquetStorage

space = DictSpace(
    NumpyComputeBackend,
    {
        "obs": BoxSpace(NumpyComputeBackend, 0.0, 1.0, np.float32, shape=(4,)),
        "action": BoxSpace(NumpyComputeBackend, -1.0, 1.0, np.float32, shape=(2,)),
    },
)

buffer = ReplayBuffer.create(
    ParquetStorage,
    space,
    cache_path="cache/replay",
    capacity=100_000,
)

Load a persisted buffer with:

restored = ReplayBuffer.load_from(
    "cache/replay",
    backend=NumpyComputeBackend,
)

Use append(value) for one unbatched step/sample at a time. The first append after creation, clear(), or the previous mark_segment_end() opens a segment implicitly.

import torch

from unienv_interface.backends.pytorch import PyTorchComputeBackend
from unienv_interface.space.spaces import BoxSpace
from unienv_data.replay_buffer import ReplayBuffer
from unienv_data.storages.pytorch import PytorchTensorStorage

space = BoxSpace(PyTorchComputeBackend, -10, 10, torch.int64, shape=(2,))
buffer = ReplayBuffer.create(
    PytorchTensorStorage,
    space,
    capacity=4,
    is_memmap=False,
)

buffer.append(torch.tensor([1, 2], dtype=torch.int64))
buffer.append(torch.tensor([3, 4], dtype=torch.int64))
buffer.mark_segment_end()

assert buffer.get_segments() == [(0, 2)]

For segment-aware storages, ReplayBuffer.get_segments() returns logical chronological half-open ranges derived from ReplayBuffer-owned physical metadata. segments_known is the flag that says whether ReplayBuffer is tracking segment boundaries itself; physical_segments stores those boundaries as inclusive physical index ranges. With fixed capacity, round-robin overwrite is supported and the ranges stay in logical buffer order.

Visibility note: the base storage append path writes through the active index and may make values visible immediately, but some implementations (notably VideoStorage) buffer data until mark_segment_end().

docs.title: Storage Backends
docs.text:
UniEnv includes multiple storage implementations, each useful for a different tradeoff.

  • ParquetStorage: columnar storage for NumPy-friendly structured data
  • HDF5Storage: HDF5-backed persistence
  • FlattenedStorage: storage built around flattened samples, often paired with another inner storage
  • PytorchTensorStorage: tensor or memmap-backed PyTorch storage
  • NPZStorage: .npz-based storage
  • ImageStorage and VideoStorage: media-oriented storage
  • DictStorage: structured composition over multiple sub-storages

The storage layer is intentionally separate from the replay-buffer semantics, so you can swap persistence formats without changing higher-level code.

VideoStorage streams frames into a temporary file for the active segment and only registers the final file on mark_segment_end(). Do not read from the active segment before finalizing it.

from unienv_data.replay_buffer import ReplayBuffer
from unienv_data.storages.video_storage import VideoStorage

rb = ReplayBuffer.create(
    VideoStorage,
    space,  # e.g. BoxSpace(..., shape=(H, W, 3))
    cache_path="cache/video",
    capacity=None,
    codec="libx264rgb",          # RGB video
    file_pixel_format="rgb24",
    buffer_pixel_format="rgb24",
    file_ext="mkv",
)

for frame in frames:
    rb.append(frame)
rb.mark_segment_end()

print(rb.storage.get_segments())  # backend-specific physical file ranges
print(rb.get_segments())          # logical half-open ranges, e.g. [(0, 3)]

For depth or other single-channel videos, prefer ffv1 with a 2D (H, W) space and a grayscale pixel format such as gray16le. For RGB video, use an RGB-capable codec such as libx264rgb (or h264/libx264 with a matching YUV pixel format like yuv420p). Set pixel formats explicitly; there is no automatic RGB fallback.

docs.title: Routing Leaves By Metadata
docs.text:
When the observation space describes its leaves with space metadata, dict_storage_kwargs_from_space builds the DictStorage layout for you: every kind == "image" (H, W, 3) uint8 leaf goes to an ImageStorage (JPEG files by default) and all other leaves to one HDF5Storage.

from unienv_data.storages import DictStorage, dict_storage_kwargs_from_space

rb = ReplayBuffer.create(
    DictStorage,
    obs_space,
    cache_path="cache/rb",
    capacity=None,
    **dict_storage_kwargs_from_space(
        obs_space,
        kind_kwargs={"image": {"format": "PNG"}},     # lossless image files
        key_storage_cls={"cameras/debug": None},      # keep this camera in the default storage
    ),
)

Storages per kind (kind_storage_cls, e.g. {"image": VideoStorage}, which then also receives the leaf's declared fps), per key (key_storage_cls) and the default storage (default_storage_cls) are all configurable, as are their keyword arguments. Channel-first or non-uint8 images stay in the default storage. create_dict_storage_from_space creates the DictStorage directly.

Storages keep the metadata of the space they are given, and ReplayBuffer.dumps / load_from persist it with the rest of the space.

docs.title: Trajectories And Samplers
docs.text:
Beyond single-transition replay:

  • StepSampler samples fixed-size batches from stored data
  • MultiprocessingSampler supports higher-throughput sampling workflows

Use these when the consumer of data is a learner or evaluation process rather than interactive environment code. Episode-level grouping now comes from ReplayBuffer segment APIs.

docs.title: Practical Advice
docs.text:
Use ReplayBuffer when you need mutation and online accumulation.

Use read-only BatchBase wrappers and integrations when the data already exists elsewhere.

Pick the storage backend based on the data you need to persist:

  • mostly numeric tabular data: ParquetStorage
  • existing HDF5 workflows: HDF5Storage
  • PyTorch-heavy pipelines or memmap tensors: PytorchTensorStorage
  • image or video artifacts: ImageStorage and VideoStorage

docs.title: Wrappers And Transformations
docs.text: UniEnv separates pure data mappings from environment-level adaptation.

docs.title: Transformations
docs.text:
Transformations live under unienv_interface.transformations.

Use them when you want to describe a mapping between spaces and their data without tying that logic to one specific environment instance.

Common examples:

  • RescaleTransformation
  • IdentityTransformation
  • DictTransformation
  • FlattenDictTransformation
  • BatchifyTransformation
  • UnBatchifyTransformation
  • CropTransformation
  • ImageResizeTransformation
  • IterativeTransformation
  • ChainedTransformation

This layer is useful when the same data mapping should be shared by wrappers, storage, or standalone preprocessing code.

docs.title: Wrappers
docs.text:
Wrappers live under unienv_interface.wrapper and operate on Env objects.

Important wrappers include:

  • ActionRescaleWrapper
  • FlattenActionWrapper
  • FlattenContextObservationWrapper
  • FrameStackWrapper
  • TimeLimitWrapper
  • ControlFrequencyLimitWrapper
  • ToBackendOrDeviceWrapper
  • BatchifyWrapper
  • UnBatchifyWrapper
  • EpisodeRenderStackWrapper
  • EpisodeVideoWrapper

docs.title: Typical Wrapper Stack
docs.text:
from unienv_interface.wrapper import (
    ActionRescaleWrapper,
    FlattenActionWrapper,
    FrameStackWrapper,
    TimeLimitWrapper,
)

env = ActionRescaleWrapper(env, new_low=-1.0, new_high=1.0)
env = FlattenActionWrapper(env)
env = FrameStackWrapper(env, obs_stack_size=3)
env = TimeLimitWrapper(env, time_limit=200)

The pattern is intentionally incremental: each wrapper changes one aspect of the interface while preserving the underlying environment contract.

docs.title: Backend Conversion
docs.text:
ToBackendOrDeviceWrapper moves the environment-facing data to another backend or device.

That is useful when:

  • the simulator produces NumPy arrays but the policy expects PyTorch tensors
  • the environment logic runs on CPU but the learner consumes data on GPU
  • you want to keep one environment implementation and swap consumers later

docs.title: Video And Render Capture
docs.text:
EpisodeRenderStackWrapper and EpisodeVideoWrapper are built for episode-level recording.

The render stack wrapper can accumulate:

  • single image streams
  • batched render outputs
  • nested mapping outputs, such as multi-camera render dictionaries

The video wrapper can then write those captured frames to disk, including one file per flattened render key for mapping-based outputs.

The recorded frames come from env.render() by default, or from the observations with frame_source="observation". When the space describing the frames (frame_space, which defaults to the observation space for observation frames) carries space metadata, only the leaves with kind == "image" are recorded, and each is converted to (H, W, 3) RGB according to its declared layout ("CHW" is moved channel-last) and format ("bgr", "rgba", "gray", ...):

wrapper = EpisodeVideoWrapper(env, store_dir="videos", frame_source="observation")
# one video per camera leaf, e.g. episode_0_step_0_key_cameras.wrist.webm

Without any kind metadata the wrappers keep their previous behaviour: every render frame is recorded as an RGB image, and for observation frames every (H, W, 3) leaf is.

docs.title: Choosing Between A Wrapper And A Transformation
docs.text:
Choose a transformation if:

  • the logic is fundamentally a space/data mapping
  • you want it to be reusable outside environment execution
  • you need to serialize or compose the mapping itself

Choose a wrapper if:

  • the logic changes how an environment is presented
  • the mapping needs access to reset, step, or render
  • you are adapting an existing environment for a downstream policy or evaluator

docs.title: UniEnv remote protocol (version 2)
docs.text: The wire contract of unienv_interface.remote, for writing clients or servers in other languages. The Python implementation is in wire.py (frames and values), protocol.py (message layout and the method allowlist) and server.py.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
A transport carries ordered, reliable frames. TCP and Unix sockets send frames back to back; WebSocket sends one frame per binary message.

u32 buffer count N | u32 JSON length L | N x u64 buffer length | L bytes UTF-8 JSON | N buffers

All integers are little-endian. The JSON is strict (no NaN / Infinity literals). Receivers reject frames over their size limit (256 MiB by default), with more than 65536 buffers, with lengths that do not add up, or whose buffers are not each referenced exactly once.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
null, booleans, integers, strings, lists and objects with string keys are plain JSON. Other values are objects with the reserved key "__t":

__t Fields Value tuple v: list tuple dict v: list of [key, value] dict with non-string keys, or with a "__t" key float v: "nan", "inf", "-inf" non-finite float bytes b: buffer index bytes nd d: dtype, s: shape, b: buffer index array, C order nd d, s, c: codec, o: codec options, b: list of buffer indices compressed array (see below) space v: space_to_json document UniEnv space graph v: n_nodes, n_edges, nodes_features, edges_features, edges GraphInstance

Dtypes are NumPy type strings with an optional byte-order prefix: b1, i1-i8, u1-u8, f2, f4, f8, c8, c16 (e.g. <f4, |u1). A shape is a list of at most 32 non-negative integers; product(shape) * itemsize must equal the buffer length. Scalars of a dtype are 0-d arrays. Nesting is limited to 64 levels. Other values (objects, strings arrays, structured dtypes, ...) cannot be sent.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Message Layout Request [id, target, method, args, kwargs] Success [id, 0, value] or [id, 0, value, updates] Error [id, 1, [exception type name, message, formatted traceback]] Event [resource name, 2, [kind, sequence, value]]

id is a client-chosen integer; responses may arrive in any order. target is a resource name, or "" for the protocol methods below. args is a list, kwargs an object. Only the methods in protocol.METHODS can be called:

Kind Methods env reset, reload (if defined), step, render world step, reset, reload, after_reset, after_reload node reset, reload, after_reset, after_reload, pre_environment_step, post_environment_step, set_next_action, get_context, get_observation, get_reward, get_termination, get_truncation, get_info, render

Calls on one registered root (and on every hosted object that shares its world) execute one at a time, in arrival order. A descriptor's world, node and children links name only objects that are hosted.

docs.title: Protocol methods
docs.text:
• hello(version=2, compress=null) must be the first request. It returns {"version": 2, "resources": {name: descriptor}}. A descriptor has kind (env, world, node), methods, attributes (name, batch_size, timings, render_mode, render_fps, supported_render_modes, has_* signals, metadata; only those present), spaces ([version, {observation_space, action_space, context_space}]), node priorities, and links: world and node (resource names) and node children ({child name: resource name}).
  • subscribe([env name]) / unsubscribe([env name]): start or stop events for that env. After every reset, reload and step, whoever called it, the server sends [name, 2, [method, sequence, result]]. Unsent events are replaced by newer ones (latest wins).

updates ({name: [version, spaces]}) carries spaces that changed since the client last saw them; the server checks after reset, reload, after_reset and after_reload calls. Clients ignore updates with a version not newer than theirs.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text: hello(compress={"image": "jpeg:90"}) asks the server to JPEG-encode (quality 90) the uint8 array leaves of results whose space has metadata["kind"] == "image", an HWC or CHW metadata["layout"] (default HWC) and 1 or 3 channels. Such a leaf is sent as {"__t": "nd", "d": "|u1", "s": shape, "c": "jpeg", "o": {"quality": 90, "layout": ..., "format": ...}, "b": [one buffer per image]} (leading dimensions are batch dimensions). Clients never compress what they send.
